title: Red Dead Redemption 2: The Last Days of the Wild West
ru: Почему вестерн от Rockstar считают одной из самых проработанных и трогательных игр в истории
text:
Some open-world games give you a map full of icons and a list of chores. Red Dead Redemption 2 gives you a world and asks you to live in it. Released in 2018 by Rockstar Games, the studio behind Grand Theft Auto, this sprawling western is still considered by many players to be one of the most detailed and emotional games ever made.

The year is 1899, and the age of the outlaw is ending. Railways, banks and government agents are steadily taming the American frontier, leaving little room for people who live outside the law. You play as Arthur Morgan, a senior member of a gang of robbers led by the charismatic Dutch van der Linde. After a robbery goes badly wrong, the gang is forced to flee, and the game follows their increasingly desperate attempts to stay one step ahead of lawmen and bounty hunters. The story is a prequel to the first Red Dead Redemption, released in 2010, so fans of that game will recognise several faces, including a younger John Marston.

Arthur is the main reason the game hits so hard. At first he seems like a classic tough gunman, loyal to Dutch and not much given to reflection. But as the story unfolds, he begins to question the man he has followed for most of his life, and his own past along with it. He keeps a journal that fills up with his thoughts and sketches as you play, revealing a mind far more thoughtful than his gruff manner suggests.

Then there is the famous level of detail. Arthur's hair and beard grow over time and need trimming. Horses must be fed, brushed and calmed down when they are frightened. Meat you carry around for too long begins to rot. People remember how you treated them, and the gang's camp feels genuinely alive, with members chatting, singing around the fire and asking you for favours. Some players find all this slow and demanding; others say it is the most immersive game they have ever played.

The world itself is spectacular, stretching from snowy mountains and misty swamps to dusty plains and Saint Denis, a crowded, smoky city clearly inspired by New Orleans. You can spend hours simply fishing, hunting, playing poker or riding through a thunderstorm with no goal at all. The music, which mixes quiet guitars with original songs that arrive at key moments, makes some of those rides unforgettable.

Red Dead Redemption 2 became one of the best-selling games of all time and won a long list of awards. But its true achievement is emotional. It is a story about loyalty, about the end of an era, and about whether a man who has done terrible things can still make his life mean something.

So take your time with it. This is a game that punishes rushing and rewards slowing down.

title: Disco Elysium: A Detective Game Without Fighting
ru: Ролевая игра, где главное оружие — диалоги, а навыки героя спорят у него в голове
text:
Most role-playing games hand you a sword. Disco Elysium hands you a hangover. You wake up half-dressed on the floor of a wrecked hostel room with no memory of who you are, not even your own name. Gradually you work out that you are a police detective, sent to the run-down district of Martinaise to investigate the death of a man found hanging from a tree behind the hostel. Then you discover that you have lost your gun, your badge and possibly your mind.

Released in 2019 by ZA/UM, a small studio formed in Estonia around the writer Robert Kurvitz, Disco Elysium is a role-playing game with almost no combat at all. Instead of fighting, you talk. You question witnesses, argue about politics, embarrass yourself in front of strangers and try, with mixed success, to piece together both the case and your own shattered identity.

The game's most famous idea is its skill system. Your character has twenty-four skills, and each of them is a voice inside your head. Logic tries to keep your reasoning straight. Empathy notices what other people are feeling. Electrochemistry, which governs your appetite for alcohol and other substances, cheerfully encourages your worst habits. Inland Empire, a kind of wild intuition, may suggest that your necktie is talking to you. These voices interrupt conversations, argue with each other and sometimes give you truly terrible advice. Putting points into a skill makes its voice louder, so building your character literally changes the way he thinks.

Success is decided by dice rolls, but failure is rarely the end of the story. Often a failed check leads somewhere funnier or stranger than success would have. It is even possible to die within the first few minutes of the game, in a way that has absolutely nothing to do with enemies.

You are not alone in all this. Your partner, Lieutenant Kim Kitsuragi, is a calm, precise officer from another precinct who observes your antics with quiet patience. He rarely judges you out loud, and as the game goes on, earning his respect becomes one of the most satisfying things you can do.

The real star, though, is the writing: a huge amount of it, often hilarious, sometimes heartbreaking and frequently philosophical. The city of Revachol, still scarred by a failed revolution decades earlier, is full of people with strong opinions, and the game lets you become a communist, an ultraliberal, a moralist or a fascist, mostly so that it can gently mock whichever path you choose. The painted art style, which looks like oil on canvas, and the moody soundtrack by the band British Sea Power complete the atmosphere.

Disco Elysium won several prizes at The Game Awards in 2019, including best narrative, and in 2021 an expanded Final Cut edition added full voice acting. It involves a lot of reading, which makes it a demanding but rewarding choice for English learners. Just don't be surprised if your own inner voices start talking back.

title: Baldur's Gate 3: Freedom as the Ultimate Feature
ru: Как ролевая игра по Dungeons & Dragons стала игрой года и почему игроки ценят её за свободу выбора
text:
In most games, the designers decide what you are allowed to do. In Baldur's Gate 3, they seem to have spent years imagining everything you might try, and then making it work. Released in full in August 2023 by the Belgian studio Larian, after nearly three years in early access, it became one of the most celebrated games of the decade and was named Game of the Year at The Game Awards.

The game is based on Dungeons & Dragons, the famous tabletop role-playing game, and follows the rules of its fifth edition. It is also a distant sequel to Baldur's Gate and Baldur's Gate II, classic computer games from around the turn of the millennium. The story begins with a nightmare. You are captured by mind flayers, monstrous creatures with tentacles for faces, who place a tiny parasite, a tadpole, inside your brain. Normally it would turn you into one of them within days. Mysteriously, it doesn't. Together with other survivors, you set out to find a cure before your luck runs out.

Those companions are the heart of the game. There is Astarion, a sharp-tongued vampire with a taste for mischief; Shadowheart, a secretive cleric; Lae'zel, a fierce warrior who considers most people beneath her; Gale, a charming wizard with a dangerous secret; and Karlach, a warm-hearted fighter with a blazing engine where her heart should be. Each has a personal story, strong opinions about your decisions, and the potential for friendship, rivalry or romance. Many players end up more attached to these characters than to the main plot.

The real magic, though, is freedom. Almost every problem has several solutions. You can fight your way through a door, pick the lock, sweet-talk the guard, sneak past, or turn into a cat and slip in through a window. You can push enemies off cliffs, throw a crate at a wizard, or cast a spell to speak with animals and pick up gossip from a dog or a squirrel. Many conversations hinge on the roll of a twenty-sided die, just like at a real tabletop session, and an unlucky roll can send the story in a completely new direction. The game rarely punishes you for being creative. More often, it rewards you with a scene the writers clearly hoped somebody would find.

Combat is turn-based and tactical, so you have time to think. The environment matters: water can be electrified, oil can be set on fire, and archers on high ground have an advantage.

All of this demanded an enormous amount of work. The game contains a vast number of fully voiced, motion-captured conversations, and the narrator, who describes your actions and thoughts like a game master at the table, became a fan favourite in her own right.

Newcomers may feel intimidated at first by all the dice, statistics and spell lists. But you don't need to know the rules of Dungeons & Dragons to enjoy it. You only need curiosity. Try something silly. Chances are, the game has an answer.

title: Why Sitcoms Still Work
about: Sitcoms: Friends, The Office, Brooklyn Nine-Nine
ru: Почему ситкомы до сих пор популярны, хотя формату больше полувека
text:
By now, the sitcom should be dead. The format is more than seventy years old, it often relies on a handful of sets and a laugh track, and its basic structure, a group of people with a small problem that gets solved within half an hour, has barely changed since the days of black-and-white television. And yet some of the most-watched shows on streaming platforms are sitcoms, many of them decades old.

The word is short for situation comedy, and the recipe is simple: put a fixed group of characters in a fixed place and let the comedy come from who they are. Early hits such as I Love Lucy in the 1950s set the pattern, and writers have been refining it ever since.

Friends shows why the recipe works. The NBC series ran from 1994 to 2004 and followed six young adults in New York who spend an improbable amount of time on the same orange sofa in a coffee shop called Central Perk. Very little happens in a typical episode: someone gets a new job, someone has a disastrous date, someone eats someone else's sandwich. But the characters are drawn so clearly that viewers feel they know them personally. New generations keep discovering the show, and for countless English learners around the world it has served as an unofficial textbook.

The Office took the formula in a different direction. The original British version, created by Ricky Gervais and Stephen Merchant, appeared in 2001; the American adaptation, with Steve Carell as the hopelessly awkward manager Michael Scott, ran from 2005 to 2013. Both are shot as fake documentaries, or mockumentaries, with no laugh track, and characters often glance at the camera when something embarrassing happens. That glance became one of the most recognisable jokes on television. It lets the audience in on the awkwardness, like a shared secret.

Brooklyn Nine-Nine, which ran from 2013 to 2021, moved the sitcom into a police station and combined fast, silly gags with surprisingly warm stories about friendship and belonging. When Fox cancelled it in 2018, fans protested loudly online, and within about a day NBC had picked it up, a rare case of an audience rescuing a show.

So why does the format survive? Part of the answer is comfort. Sitcoms offer low stakes and familiar rhythms; whatever goes wrong will usually be fixed by the end of the episode. Many people put them on in the background, or watch them before falling asleep, precisely because nothing truly terrible will happen. Another part is what writers call the found family: a group of friends or colleagues who, despite all their flaws, always show up for each other. In a lonely world, that is a powerful fantasy.

Finally, sitcoms are built on character rather than plot, so they age surprisingly well. Fashions change, and phones get smaller and then bigger again, but a friend who keeps making bad decisions is funny in any decade. That may be the real secret: we come back not for the story, but for the people.

title: The Streaming Wars
about: Netflix, Disney+, Max and the battle for viewers
ru: Как стриминговые сервисы воюют за зрителя и что это значит для нас
text:
Not so long ago, watching something online was simple. You had Netflix, and Netflix seemed to have almost everything. Today, many viewers pay for three, four or even five services and still cannot find the show they want. Welcome to the streaming wars.

Netflix did start the revolution, though not in the way most people remember. It began in the late 1990s as a company that posted DVDs to its customers. In 2007, it added online streaming, and in 2013 it released House of Cards, a political drama that proved a streaming company could make prestige television of its own. It also popularised a new habit: releasing every episode of a season at once. The word binge-watching soon entered everyday language.

For a while, the big Hollywood studios were happy to sell Netflix their old films and series. Then they realised they were feeding a rival. One after another, they launched services of their own. Disney+ arrived in 2019, packed with Marvel, Star Wars, Pixar and Disney classics. Apple TV+ launched the same year with a small but polished collection of originals. HBO Max appeared in 2020, was renamed Max in 2023, and went back to being HBO Max in 2025. Amazon, Paramount, NBCUniversal and others joined the fight as well.

The result was a scramble for content. Shows that had lived on Netflix for years began to disappear as their owners took them back. In the United States, Friends moved to HBO Max, and The Office left for Peacock, NBCUniversal's own service. Companies spent huge sums on exclusive series, hoping a single hit would bring in millions of new subscribers.

For viewers, this has been a mixed blessing. On the one hand, there is more ambitious television than ever, from expensive fantasy epics to small foreign dramas that would never have reached a global audience before. A Korean thriller like Squid Game could become a worldwide phenomenon almost overnight. On the other hand, the cost adds up, and keeping track of which show lives where has become a hobby in itself. Many people now subscribe to a service for a single season of a single series and then cancel, a behaviour the industry calls churn.

The platforms have responded by changing tactics. Most now offer cheaper plans with advertisements, which look suspiciously like old-fashioned television. In 2023, Netflix began cracking down on people sharing passwords outside their household. Some companies have started bundling their services together, offering several platforms for one price, which looks remarkably like the cable packages that streaming was supposed to replace.

So who will win? Probably no single company. The likeliest outcome is a handful of giants surrounded by smaller specialist services, all competing with free video platforms such as YouTube for the same hours of our attention.

For now, the most useful skill for a modern viewer may be patience. Subscribe, watch what you want, cancel, and come back when the next must-see show arrives. In the streaming wars, the audience has more power than it thinks.

title: How an Animated Film Is Made
about: The making of a computer-animated feature
ru: Этапы создания полнометражного анимационного фильма — от идеи до рендеринга
text:
A ninety-minute computer-animated film can take four years or more to make and involve hundreds of artists, engineers and technicians. Almost nothing on screen happens by accident. Every blade of grass, every flicker of an eyelid and every ray of light was decided by someone. So how does a blank page become a finished film?

It starts, unsurprisingly, with a story. A director or a small team pitches an idea, and writers develop it into an outline and, eventually, a script. In animation, though, the script is only the beginning. Story artists work the film out visually, drawing thousands of rough sketches called storyboards, almost like a giant comic book. These drawings are then edited together with temporary voices, music and sound effects to create a story reel, a rough, cheap version of the entire film. The studio watches it again and again, rewriting and redrawing whatever doesn't work. Throwing away a sketch costs far less than throwing away a finished scene, so the biggest changes happen at this stage, sometimes years before release.

Voice actors are usually recorded early, because animators need the performance to shape the movements and expressions. Actors often record their lines alone in a booth, without the rest of the cast, and the editors assemble the conversations later.

Meanwhile, the art department designs the world: characters, costumes, locations, colours and mood. Then the computer work begins. Modellers build every character and object as a three-dimensional digital sculpture. Riggers give those models a hidden skeleton of controls, so that an animator can bend an elbow, raise an eyebrow or twist a smile. Layout artists place virtual cameras in each scene, choosing angles and lenses just as a cinematographer would on a real set.

Only then do the animators bring the characters to life. Films usually run at twenty-four frames per second, and a skilled animator may produce just a few seconds of finished footage in a week. Many of them film themselves acting out a scene for reference, which is why animation studios are full of people pulling strange faces at cameras.

Some things are too complex to move by hand. Hair, fur, cloth, water and smoke are handled by simulation specialists using physics-based software. Fur and curly hair have been particularly tough challenges: Sulley's fur in Pixar's Monsters, Inc. and Merida's wild red curls in Brave both required new technology.

Next comes lighting, which can completely change the emotional tone of a shot, followed by rendering, the process in which computers calculate the final images. A single frame can take hours to render, so studios rely on render farms, rooms full of powerful computers working day and night. The rendered layers are combined in a stage called compositing, and finally sound designers and composers add the effects and music that make the world feel real.

All of this is surprisingly recent. Only in 1995 did Pixar's Toy Story become the first feature-length film animated entirely by computer. The tools have changed enormously since then, but the goal has not: hundreds of people working for years to make something look effortless.

title: Dubbing vs Subtitles
about: Dubbing, subtitles and voice-over around the world
ru: Дубляж или субтитры: что выбирают разные страны и почему спор не утихает
text:
Ask a German and a Swede how they prefer to watch foreign films, and you might start an argument. Across the world, audiences have strong opinions about whether a film should be dubbed, subtitled or voiced over, and their habits often reveal as much about history and economics as about taste.

There are three main options. In full dubbing, the original voices are replaced by actors speaking the local language, ideally timed to match the lip movements on screen. With subtitles, you hear the original soundtrack and read a translation at the bottom of the screen. Voice-over sits in between: the original actors can still be heard faintly in the background while one or more local voices read a translation on top.

Germany, France, Italy and Spain have long traditions of dubbing, and in these countries it is a respected profession. A popular foreign star often keeps the same local voice actor for decades, and audiences grow so attached to that voice that replacing it can cause an outcry. Dubbing is expensive, but large countries have audiences big enough to pay for it.

Smaller markets such as the Netherlands, Portugal and the Nordic countries have traditionally relied on subtitles, partly because dubbing for a small audience never made financial sense. A side effect that people often mention is that children there grow up hearing English every day, and many end up speaking it remarkably well. Subtitles are not the only reason, of course, but they very likely help.

Poland is famous for a third tradition, the lektor: a single, usually male voice that calmly reads the dialogue of every character, from hero to villain, with very little emotion. Russian-speaking viewers know something similar from the era of pirated videotapes, when one translator's unmistakable voice could carry an entire action film. Today, Russian cinemas mostly show fully dubbed films, while online, multi-voice voice-overs produced by studios and fan groups are common.

Each method has its defenders. Supporters of dubbing say it lets you focus on the images instead of reading, and that it makes films accessible to children, older people and anyone with poor eyesight. Supporters of subtitles argue that an actor's voice is half of the performance, and that replacing it means watching a different film. Subtitles have weaknesses too. They must shorten dialogue to fit the screen, so jokes and nuances often get lost. When the Korean series Squid Game became a global hit in 2021, some Korean speakers complained that the English captions changed the meaning of certain lines.

Streaming has reshaped the debate. A single series can now be released with dozens of audio tracks and subtitle options, and younger viewers increasingly choose subtitles even in countries with a strong dubbing tradition. Artificial intelligence is also entering the field, with tools that can make an actor appear to speak another language in their own voice, a development that excites studios and worries professional voice actors.

There is no single right answer, only habits. But if you are learning English, the choice is easy: original audio, English subtitles and a little patience.

title: Learning English with TV Shows
about: Using series to improve your English
ru: Как с пользой учить английский по сериалам — практические советы
text:
Every English learner has heard the advice: just watch series in English. It sounds wonderful. You lie on the sofa, enjoy a good story and slowly soak up the language. The reality is a little more complicated. TV can be one of the most effective ways to improve your English, but only if you use it in the right way.

The first step is choosing the right show. Researchers who study reading suggest that we understand a text comfortably only when we know around ninety-five percent of its words, or more. Dialogue on screen works in a similar way: if you miss every third word, you will not learn much; you will just get tired. So start with something manageable. Sitcoms are a classic choice, because episodes are short, situations are familiar and the dialogue is about everyday life. Shows you have already seen in your own language are even better, since you know the plot and can focus on how things are said. Save fast-talking legal dramas, historical epics and anything with strong regional accents for later.

Next, think about subtitles. Subtitles in your native language feel comfortable, but your brain will read them instead of listening, and you will learn surprisingly little. English subtitles are a much better compromise: they connect the sounds you hear with the words you see, and they help you notice how fast speech blurs words together. Once you feel more confident, try switching them off for scenes you have already watched.

The biggest difference, however, comes from active watching. Passive viewing is pleasant, but mostly it trains your patience. Try this instead: watch an episode once for fun, then pick a short scene of two or three minutes and really work with it. Pause after each line. Repeat it out loud, copying the rhythm and intonation, a technique known as shadowing. Write down useful phrases, not just single words: “I'll pass”, “that's on me”, “you've got to be kidding me”. Ready-made chunks like these are exactly what makes speech sound natural, and you will rarely find them in a textbook.

Keep these phrases in a notebook or a flashcard app, and review them regularly. Ten phrases you actually remember are worth more than a hundred you wrote down once and forgot.

It also pays to vary your diet. British, American, Australian and Irish English sound very different, and so do characters from different backgrounds and generations. Documentaries and nature programmes, with their clear, careful narration, are excellent for listening practice.

Finally, be realistic and kind to yourself. You will not understand everything, and that is perfectly normal. Native speakers miss lines too, which is one reason so many of them now watch with subtitles switched on. Progress with TV feels slow at first and then suddenly becomes obvious: one day you realise you laughed at a joke before you had time to read it. That moment is worth all the pausing and rewinding.

So go ahead and binge. Just make sure that, at least some of the time, you are doing more than lying on the sofa.

title: Storytelling in Video Games
about: Narrative in games: The Last of Us, Mass Effect, Disco Elysium
ru: Чем рассказ истории в играх отличается от кино и книг
text:
Films show you a story. Books ask you to imagine one. Video games do something stranger: they hand you the controller and ask you to take part. That simple difference changes almost everything about how a story can be told.

Take The Last of Us, released by Naughty Dog in 2013. On paper, its plot sounds familiar: after a fungal infection has destroyed civilisation, a hardened smuggler named Joel must escort a teenage girl, Ellie, across a ruined United States. What makes it unforgettable is that you do not simply watch Joel protect Ellie. You do it yourself, hour after hour, through dark buildings and desperate fights. By the time the story reaches its hardest moments, you have been part of that relationship for so long that the emotional weight lands on you personally. The quiet moments are just as powerful: a short, almost wordless encounter with a group of giraffes in an abandoned city is remembered by many players more vividly than any battle.

Mass Effect, the science-fiction trilogy from BioWare that began in 2007, took a different approach: choice. As Commander Shepard, you make decisions that shape the fate of individual characters and entire species. Crucially, you could carry your saved game from one instalment to the next, so a decision made in the first game might come back to haunt you years later in the third.

Disco Elysium, released in 2019, pushed in yet another direction. It has almost no combat; the story unfolds through dialogue, and the hero's skills speak to him as voices in his head. In this game, failure does not lead to a game over screen but to a new, often funnier branch of the story.

These games point to tools that are unique to the medium. One is agency, the feeling that your actions really matter. Another is environmental storytelling. Instead of explaining everything in cutscenes, designers leave clues in the world itself: a child's drawing on a wall, a barricaded door, a note written by someone who did not make it. Players piece the story together on their own, so it feels like a discovery rather than a lecture.

Games also face problems that films never have to deal with. Critics sometimes talk about ludonarrative dissonance, a term coined by the designer Clint Hocking in 2007. It describes what happens when the story says one thing and the gameplay says another, for example when a hero is presented as gentle and kind in cutscenes but casually defeats hundreds of enemies in between. And real choice is expensive, because every branch has to be written, recorded and tested, which is why many games offer paths that split briefly and then quietly join up again.

Still, game stories are no longer an afterthought. Games now attract famous actors, celebrated writers and serious critics, and The Last of Us has even become a successful television series. Yet the most powerful moments in games remain the ones only games can create: those in which you are not just watching a story, but living inside it.

title: Fandoms and Fan Theories
about: Fan communities, fan theories and fan fiction
ru: Как устроены фанатские сообщества и почему люди так любят теории
text:
Somewhere right now, someone is writing a ten-thousand-word essay explaining why a minor character in a cartoon is secretly the villain. Somewhere else, a group of strangers is arguing, politely or not so politely, about whether two characters should have ended up together. Welcome to fandom: the communities of passionate fans that grow up around films, series, books, games and bands.

Fandom is not new. In 1893, readers were so upset when Arthur Conan Doyle killed off Sherlock Holmes that the author eventually brought his detective back. In the 1960s, fans of Star Trek were already producing homemade magazines, known as fanzines, full of their own stories and essays, and they organised a famous letter-writing campaign to save the series from cancellation. What the internet changed was scale and speed. Forums, Reddit, Discord servers and fan wikis allow millions of people to discuss every detail of a story within minutes of its release.

One of the most popular fan activities is theorising. A fan theory is an unofficial explanation of a mystery in a story, or a bold prediction about what will happen next. Some theories are argued with the care of a legal case. Others are gloriously absurd. One well-known theory claims that all Pixar films take place in a single shared universe; another, which went viral in 2015, argued that the clumsy Jar Jar Binks from the Star Wars prequels was secretly a powerful villain in disguise. Neither was ever confirmed, but both provided endless entertainment.

Why do people love theories so much? Partly because they turn watching into an activity. Instead of waiting passively for the next episode, fans become detectives, collecting clues and testing ideas against each other.

Another huge part of fandom is fan fiction: stories written by fans using existing characters and worlds. It ranges from tiny jokes to novels longer than the originals, and it covers every genre imaginable. Some professional careers began this way; the bestselling romance Fifty Shades of Grey started life as fan fiction inspired by Twilight. In 2019, the volunteer-run fan fiction website Archive of Our Own even received a Hugo Award, one of the most prestigious prizes in science fiction. Fans also produce art, music, videos and cosplay, dressing up as their favourite characters at conventions.

Fandom has its own vocabulary, too. To ship two characters means to want them in a romantic relationship; the word comes from relationship and spread among fans of The X-Files in the 1990s. Canon is what officially happens in the story, while headcanon is what an individual fan privately believes.

Of course, there is a darker side. Passionate communities can turn hostile, attacking actors, writers or other fans who disagree with them. Coordinated campaigns that flood a film or game with negative reviews, known as review bombing, have become a familiar problem.

At its best, though, fandom is about connection. It turns watching or reading, usually a solitary experience, into a shared conversation. And it reminds creators that once a story is released into the world, it no longer belongs only to them.

title: Spoilers and Why We Hate Them
ru: Почему спойлеры так раздражают и действительно ли они портят удовольствие
text:
You have been avoiding the internet for three days. You muted keywords, left two group chats and walked out of the office kitchen with your fingers in your ears. Then, on the bus, a stranger's phone screen tells you exactly who dies. Few small disasters feel quite so personal.

The word “spoiler” has been around for decades, but spoiler culture as we know it is a product of the internet. When a film opened in cinemas, or an episode aired once a week, most people saw it at roughly the same time. Today one viewer finishes a whole season on the night it drops, while another is still on episode two a month later, and both of them are on the same social networks. The gap between them is where spoilers live.

So why do they hurt so much? Part of the answer is control. A story is built to deliver its surprises in a particular order, and a spoiler takes that order out of your hands. There is something social going on, too. Being spoiled can feel like being left out of a shared experience, as if everyone else got to open the present and you were handed the empty box.

Here is the twist, though: science is not entirely on our side. In a well-known 2011 study at the University of California, San Diego, researchers gave people short stories to read, some with the ending revealed in advance and some without. On average, readers actually enjoyed the spoiled versions slightly more. One explanation is that knowing where a story is going frees you to notice how it gets there — the craft, the foreshadowing, the small details you would otherwise rush past.

That fits with how we treat our favorite films. Nobody refuses to rewatch a classic because they know how it ends. Some of the most famous twists in cinema, like the big reveal in The Empire Strikes Back, are now so widely known that people learn them years before they see the film, and the scenes still land.

Still, not every story survives the experiment. A mystery built entirely around one question, or a horror film that depends on the unknown, can lose much of its power. And that study measured short stories, not a ten-year relationship with a TV series. When you have invested a decade in a set of characters, the moment of discovery is part of what you signed up for.

That is why the internet has developed its own etiquette: spoiler tags, warnings in headlines and an unwritten rule that a few days of silence after a premiere is simply good manners. Whether or not spoilers really ruin stories, they clearly ruin something — the right to be surprised on your own terms. So the next time you are tempted to post that shocking scene, ask yourself one question: is it worth losing a friend over?

title: The Age of Binge-Watching
about: Binge-watching and how streaming changed our habits
ru: Как запойный просмотр сериалов изменил и зрителей, и сами сериалы
text:
“Just one more episode” may be the most dishonest sentence of the twenty-first century. We say it at eleven at night, and suddenly it is three in the morning, the credits are rolling on episode eight and the screen is politely asking whether we are still watching.

People have always found ways to watch a lot of television at once. Fans held marathons with boxed DVD sets, and cable channels ran whole seasons of old sitcoms on holiday weekends. But binge-watching as a normal, everyday habit arrived with streaming. In 2013 Netflix released every episode of its political drama House of Cards on the same day. The idea seemed strange at the time — why give away a whole season at once? — but viewers loved it, and the model spread quickly. By 2015 “binge-watch” was common enough to be named word of the year by Collins Dictionary.

Streaming services also designed their apps to keep us in our seats. Autoplay starts the next episode a few seconds after the last one ends. The “skip intro” button removes the natural pause in which you might have stood up and gone to bed. Even the recap at the start of an episode becomes pointless when you saw the previous one five minutes ago.

The shows themselves began to change, too. A traditional network series was designed to be watched once a week, so each episode needed a clear beginning, middle and end, plus a reminder of who everyone was. Streaming dramas are often written more like very long films, split into chapters. Some critics say this has made TV richer, with slower storytelling and more complex characters. Others complain that many series now feel like a two-hour story stretched over ten hours, with a strong start, a tired middle and an ending designed mainly to set up the next season.

There is a social cost as well. When everyone watched the same episode on the same night, the next day at work turned into a group discussion. Now your colleague has already finished the season while you are still meeting the characters, and any conversation about it means tiptoeing around spoilers.

Interestingly, the industry has partly swung back. Disney+ released The Mandalorian one episode a week, giving fans time to argue online and build theories between episodes. Netflix itself has split big seasons of Stranger Things into separate volumes. A show that stays in the conversation for two months, it turns out, can be worth more than one that people devour in a single weekend and then forget.

So binge-watching has not killed the weekly episode. Instead, we now have a choice — which means the only thing standing between you and episode nine is your own willpower. Good luck with that.

title: The Rise of Anime in the West
about: Anime outside Japan: from Astro Boy to Demon Slayer
ru: Как японская анимация прошла путь от нишевого хобби до мейнстрима на Западе
text:
Thirty years ago, admitting in the West that you watched Japanese cartoons could earn you a strange look. Today anime films top box-office charts, streaming services fight over the rights to new series, and you can buy Naruto socks in an ordinary supermarket. How did a niche hobby become part of the mainstream?

The story starts surprisingly early. In 1963, Osamu Tezuka's Astro Boy, about a robot boy with rockets in his feet, was dubbed into English and shown on American television. A few years later came Speed Racer. Most young viewers had no idea these shows were Japanese at all. Names were changed, and scenes that seemed too violent or too local were cut, so that the cartoons looked as American as possible.

For many Western fans, the real turning point was Akira, Katsuhiro Otomo's 1988 film about psychic powers and biker gangs in a ruined future Tokyo. It was dark, detailed and clearly not made for children. Copies spread through specialist video shops and university film clubs, and a generation of viewers realized that animation could be as serious and ambitious as any live-action film.

Then came the late 1990s, and the floodgates opened. Pokémon arrived with its games, trading cards and TV series and became a worldwide craze. In the US, Cartoon Network's Toonami block brought shows like Dragon Ball Z and Sailor Moon to after-school audiences. Meanwhile, fans who wanted more were trading tapes with homemade subtitles, known as fansubs, often years before an official release.

Hayao Miyazaki and Studio Ghibli gave anime a different kind of respect. When Spirited Away won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature in 2003, even people who would never call themselves fans started paying attention, and critics began describing Miyazaki as one of the greatest animators who had ever lived.

The internet did the rest. Legal streaming sites such as Crunchyroll began offering new episodes with subtitles within hours of their Japanese broadcast — a practice called simulcasting — and Netflix started paying for its own anime. Fans no longer had to wait, hunt for tapes or pay import prices.

The results became impossible to ignore in 2020, when Demon Slayer: Mugen Train became, at the time, the highest-grossing film in Japanese history and went on to fill cinemas around the world. Series like Attack on Titan, Jujutsu Kaisen and One Piece have trended worldwide the moment new episodes appeared, and in 2023 Netflix even turned One Piece into a live-action show.

Interestingly, anime did not have to change itself to fit Western tastes. If anything, the opposite happened: Western audiences learned to love its long stories, its strange humor and its willingness to make grown adults cry over a cartoon. Those strange looks have mostly disappeared. The question now is not whether you watch anime, but which one.

title: The Voices Behind the Cartoons
about: Voice actors: Mel Blanc, Dan Castellaneta, Tom Kenny
ru: Кто такие актёры озвучивания и почему их работа сложнее, чем кажется
text:
Close your eyes and think of Bugs Bunny. You can probably hear him before you can picture him: that relaxed, slightly cheeky New York voice asking what's up. That voice belonged to Mel Blanc, and for much of the twentieth century he was one of the most-heard performers on the planet, even though most people could not have picked his face out of a crowd.

Blanc was known as “The Man of a Thousand Voices”, and he earned the title. Working for Warner Bros., he voiced not only Bugs but also Daffy Duck, Porky Pig, Tweety and many more. Each character needed its own rhythm, pitch and personality, and Blanc often had to jump between them in a single recording session. When he died in 1989, his gravestone carried Porky Pig's famous goodbye, the line that closed so many of the cartoons he had worked on.

Voice acting looks easy from the outside. You stand in a small room, read from a script and go home without ever putting on makeup. In reality, it is acting with one hand tied behind your back. There is no costume, no set and often no other actor to play against, because in American animation performers usually record their lines alone. Everything — fear, love, a joke that has to land — must be carried by the voice. Many actors finish their sessions physically exhausted, especially after a day of screaming, crying or playing a monster.

Then there is endurance. Dan Castellaneta has voiced Homer Simpson since the late 1980s, when the family first appeared in short segments on The Tracey Ullman Show. Over the decades he has also played Grampa Simpson, Krusty the Clown and Barney Gumble, sometimes in conversation with each other. Homer's famous grunt of frustration, “D'oh!”, became so widely used that it ended up in the Oxford English Dictionary.

Tom Kenny is another voice that has shaped childhoods. Since 1999 he has played SpongeBob SquarePants, giving the sponge his high-pitched, wildly enthusiastic laugh. Fans of Adventure Time also know him as the Ice King, a completely different character: lonely, ridiculous and, eventually, surprisingly sad. Hearing the two back to back is a good lesson in how much range a single throat can have.

Today voice acting is a bigger industry than ever, with work in films, television, anime dubbing, audiobooks and especially video games, where a single role can involve thousands of lines. Hollywood stars are increasingly hired for animated films, which some professional voice actors find frustrating, since a famous name does not always mean a great vocal performance.

The best voice actors share one strange talent: they disappear. When the job is done well, you do not think about a person in a booth at all. You simply believe that a rabbit, a sponge or a bald man on a couch is talking directly to you.

title: Why Villains Steal the Show
about: Villains in film: Scar, Hans Gruber, the Joker, Loki
ru: Почему злодеи часто интереснее героев и чем запоминаются лучшие из них
text:
Ask people to name their favorite character from a big movie, and a surprising number will pick the one who is trying to ruin everyone's day. Villains get the best lines, the best costumes and often the best scenes. Why do we enjoy the bad guys so much?

One reason is simple: the villain usually drives the story. Heroes often react, but villains act. They have a plan, and the plot exists largely because someone is trying to stop it. That gives a good villain a sense of purpose and confidence that heroes, busy being decent and full of doubt, rarely get to show.

Look at Scar in Disney's The Lion King (1994). Young Simba mostly wants to have fun, while Scar is bitter, intelligent and dryly funny. Voiced by Jeremy Irons with lazy, aristocratic contempt, he gets one of the darkest musical numbers Disney had ever made, complete with marching hyenas. Children were scared of him; their parents secretly enjoyed every line.

Or take Hans Gruber in Die Hard (1988). Alan Rickman, in his first feature film, played him not as a screaming maniac but as a calm, well-dressed professional who is clearly the smartest person in the building. The audience almost admires his plan, which makes Bruce Willis's tired, barefoot hero look even more desperate. Many critics still rank Gruber among the greatest movie villains of all time.

Some villains are frightening precisely because they have no plan we can understand. Heath Ledger's Joker in The Dark Knight (2008) tells contradictory stories about his past and seems to want nothing except chaos. Ledger died before the film came out, and he won a posthumous Academy Award — one given after the winner's death — for Best Supporting Actor. His performance changed what audiences expected from comic-book movies.

Then there is the villain who becomes too popular to stay a villain. Tom Hiddleston's Loki first appeared in Thor (2011) as a jealous younger brother with a gift for lies. Fans loved his mix of charm, wounded pride and theatrical evil so much that Marvel kept bringing him back, and in 2021 it gave him his own series, simply called Loki.

What these characters share is not just evil but personality. A great villain usually believes he is right, or at least has a reason we can understand: jealousy, ambition, a sense of injustice. We may not agree with him, but we recognize something human in him — and that is more disturbing than any monster.

There is also the guilty pleasure of watching someone break the rules we follow every day. In real life, we cannot insult our boss with perfect timing or take over a skyscraper. On screen, for two hours, we can enjoy someone who does exactly that with style, knowing that the hero will probably win in the end. Probably.

Villains get more screen time than heroes

Nora: Thank you. Seriously. I don't even know your name.

Pilot: Jonah Reyes. Two tons of frozen noodles. And I've been flying for nineteen hours, so I'd really like to sleep in a real bed.
Control: Sleep is not an official reason. Please choose from the list: trade, repair or medical.
Pilot: Fine. Trade. The noodles are for trade.
Control: Thank you. Your ship hasn't visited this station before. Have you filled in form 12-B?
Pilot: I've never even heard of form 12-B.
Control: It was sent to all pilots last month. It's forty pages long.
Pilot: Forty pages? I can barely keep my eyes open. I'm not reading forty pages.
Control: Then I'm afraid you'll have to wait in the holding area until it has been completed.
Pilot: How many ships are waiting there right now?
Control: Six. The first one arrived on Tuesday.
Pilot: It's Friday! Come on, there must be something you can do. My noodles are starting to defrost.
Control: Did you say noodles? What kind?
Pilot: Spicy chicken, mostly. Some beef. Why?
Control: The station canteen ran out of food three days ago. Everyone up here has been living on protein bars.
Pilot: So if I gave the canteen a box or two, would form 12-B suddenly get a bit shorter?
Control: I can't accept gifts, pilot. However, I can register your cargo as emergency supplies. Emergency ships don't need the form.
Pilot: You're a hero. Which bay?
Control: Bay seven. Welcome to Kessler Station, Mr Reyes.
Pilot: Kessler? Wait. My noodles are supposed to go to Kepler Station!
Control: Kepler is only six hours away. But I'm afraid they'll want form 12-B too.

title: My Horse Is on the Roof
ru: Игрок жалуется в поддержку на странный баг с лошадью, а агент пытается разобраться
text:
Player: Hi. I need help. My horse is on the roof of the blacksmith's house and it won't come down.
Agent: Hello, and thanks for contacting support! I'm sorry to hear that. Could you tell me how the horse got up there?
Player: That's what I'd like to know! I left it outside the shop for two minutes. When I came out, it was on the roof.
Agent: I see. Have you tried calling it with the whistle?
Player: Of course. Every time I whistle, it looks at me and then turns around.
Agent: Interesting. Have you installed any mods recently?
Player: Just one. It makes the grass look nicer. That's all, I promise.
Agent: Grass mods have caused some strange problems before. Could you turn it off and load your last save?
Player: I've already done that. Now there are two horses on the roof.
Agent: Two? Is the second one also yours?
Player: No idea. It's wearing a little hat. My horse has never worn a hat in its life.
Agent: Okay, I've passed this on to our developers. While we wait, can you get onto the roof yourself?
Player: Only by climbing the chimney, and every time I try, I fall off and lose half my health.
Agent: In that case, you can get a new horse at the stables. It's free for players who have been affected by this bug.
Player: But I don't want a new horse. That horse and I have been through everything. Dragons, bandits, a terrible wedding...
Agent: I understand. Oh, our developers have just replied.
Player: And? Can they fix it?
Agent: They say it isn't a bug. Since the last update, horses can climb if they're left alone and get bored.
Player: Bored? So it's my fault?
Agent: In a way, yes. They recommend spending more time with your horse. Maybe brush it now and then.
Player: Fine. And what about the one in the hat?
Agent: That's its new friend. The developers say please don't separate them.

title: Half-Time Talk
ru: Команда проигрывает 0:2, и тренер в перерыве пытается всё изменить
text:
Coach: Sit down, all of you. Nobody touches the water until I've finished talking.
Kai: Coach, it's not that bad. We've had a few chances.
Coach: A few chances? We're losing two-nil to a team that hasn't won a match since March!
Leo: Their goalkeeper is really good, though. He's saved everything.
Coach: He's saved two shots, Leo. Two. Both of them went straight into his hands.
Rico: To be fair, I've been completely alone up front. Nobody has passed me the ball.
Tomas: Because you're always offside! The linesman knows your name by now.
Coach: Enough. Tomas, what happened with the first goal?
Tomas: I was trying to pass it back to our keeper. The wind took it.
Coach: There is no wind today. The flags haven't moved once.
Kai: And the second goal was a penalty. Their striker fell over like he'd been shot.
Leo: You did pull his shirt, Kai. I saw it from the other side of the pitch.
Coach: Listen. If we keep playing like strangers, we'll lose four-nil. So we're changing everything.
Rico: Changing what exactly?
Coach: Tomas moves to the middle. Leo, you play wide on the left. And Rico, you stay onside for once in your life.
Rico: What if they score again?
Coach: Then at least we'll lose with style. But if we score early, they'll panic. They aren't used to winning.
Kai: Coach is right. Come on, boys, forty-five minutes. We've come back from worse.
Leo: Have we? When?
Kai: Never. But there's a first time for everything.
Coach: Good. Now go out there and... Wait. Why is Tomas wearing goalkeeper gloves?
Tomas: Our keeper's locked himself in the toilet. He says he isn't coming out until we start defending.

title: A Bargain in the Dark
about: RPG · торг с контрабандистом в порту
ru: Героиня торгуется с хитрым контрабандистом за карту, которая нужна для квеста
text:
Smuggler: You're late. I don't like customers who are late. It makes me nervous.
Irina: The harbour guards were checking every boat. I had to wait until they'd gone. Have you got the map?
Smuggler: Maybe. It depends on what you've brought me.
Irina: Two hundred gold, like we agreed.
Smuggler: Ah, but that was yesterday. Since then, three other people have asked about this map. The price has gone up.
Irina: Gone up to what?
Smuggler: Six hundred. And I'm only saying six hundred because I like your face.
Irina: Six hundred? For an old piece of paper that's been sitting in a fish crate?
Smuggler: An old piece of paper that shows the way into the Sunken Library. Without it, you'll drown in the tunnels like everybody else.
Irina: Then let me see it first. I'm not paying for a drawing of your grandmother's garden.
Smuggler: Look, but don't touch. See the red line? That's the only safe path through the caves.
Irina: Hmm. The ink is still wet in this corner.
Smuggler: It's very damp down here. Everything's wet. Even my bread.
Irina: Here's my offer. Three hundred gold, and I don't tell the guards about the boxes behind you.
Smuggler: What boxes? Those are... apples.
Irina: Apples don't usually have the king's seal on them.
Smuggler: All right, all right. Three hundred, and you never saw me.
Irina: Pleasure doing business. Here's your money. Count it if you like.
Smuggler: I will. Wait a minute. Half of these coins are chocolate.
Irina: And half of your map is still wet. I'd say that makes us even.

title: Raid Night

title: The Four Crystals
ru: Чудаковатый учёный-NPC объясняет игроку загадку с кристаллами, от которой зависит дверь в лабораторию
text:
Professor: Ah, a visitor! Don't touch anything. Especially the glowing jar. Especially that one.
Alex: I wasn't going to. I just need to get through that door. The villagers say the cure is in your lab.
Professor: The cure! Yes, it's in the storeroom behind that door, with all my food. Unfortunately, the door is locked by my greatest invention: the Crystal Lock.
Alex: Can't you just open it?
Professor: I could, if I remembered the order. I've changed it so often that I've forgotten it myself.
Alex: Great. So how do we work it out?
Professor: I wrote down some clues, just in case. Here's the first one: green always goes first.
Alex: Easy. Green in the first holder. What else?
Professor: Red and blue have had an argument. They must never stand next to each other.
Alex: Crystals can have arguments?
Professor: These ones can. They've been sulking since Tuesday. Last clue: blue likes to be close to the window.
Alex: The window's on the right, so blue goes in the last holder.
Professor: Very good! That leaves red and yellow, and two empty holders.
Alex: If red goes next to blue, they'll start arguing again. So yellow goes third, and red goes second.
Professor: Green, red, yellow, blue. Brilliant! Put them in, quickly, before they change their minds.
Alex: Done. Something's humming... The door's opening!
Professor: Marvellous! You've solved in five minutes what I couldn't solve in three weeks.
Alex: Three weeks? Then how have you been getting food?
Professor: Through the back door, of course. It's never been locked.
Alex: There's a back door? Does it go into the same room?
Professor: Yes. But it's much less fun.

title: The Iron Chancellor
ru: Посланник героя пытается убедить холодного лидера фракции вступить в союз против общего врага
text:
Chancellor: You rode for six days to see me. I'll give you six minutes. One per day seems fair.
Envoy: Generous. I'll only need four. The Ash Legion crossed the river on Monday. They burned Harrowgate on Wednesday.
Chancellor: Harrowgate was a village of goat farmers who owed me taxes. Forgive me if I'm not in mourning.
Envoy: They won't stop at goats. Your city is next, and you know it.
Chancellor: My walls have stood for three hundred years. What makes this rabble so special?
Envoy: Siege engines. Twelve of them, built by engineers who used to work for you.
Chancellor: Ah. So that's where they went. I did wonder.
Envoy: My queen is offering an alliance. Our cavalry, your archers. We meet the Legion in the open, long before they reach your gates.
Chancellor: And when the dust settles, your queen has an army camped on my doorstep. That sounds like a different kind of siege.
Envoy: She'll sign a treaty. Every one of her soldiers back across the border within forty days.
Chancellor: A treaty is just a promise with better handwriting.
Envoy: Then what would convince you?
Chancellor: The silver mines at Kell. All three of them.
Envoy: That's not a negotiation. That's a robbery.
Chancellor: You're the one asking for help, envoy. Beggars can't be choosers.
Envoy: One mine. And my queen gives up her share of the river tolls for ten years.
Chancellor: Two mines, and the tolls for twenty.
Envoy: Two mines, fifteen years, and you lead the left flank in person.
Chancellor: In person? You want me on a horse?
Envoy: My queen says a ruler who won't ride out with his men isn't worth riding out for.
Chancellor: Your queen has a sharp tongue. Fine. Tell her she has a deal.
Envoy: Just like that? A minute ago you were digging your heels in.
Chancellor: My scouts told me about those siege engines on Tuesday. I was always going to say yes. I just wanted to see how much you'd give me first.
Envoy: So I could have walked in here and simply asked?
Chancellor: You could have. But you started bargaining, so I let you. Next time, envoy, open with “please”. It's much cheaper.

title: The Missing Hour
ru: Детектив допрашивает вежливого дворецкого и ловит его на противоречии в показаниях
text:
Detective: Sit down, Mr. Hale. Tea? No? Fair enough, it's terrible tea.
Butler: So I've noticed. I've been meaning to speak to the cook about it for eleven years.
Detective: Let's talk about last night instead. Lord Ashby says something went missing from the gallery between nine and ten.
Butler: So I understand. A shocking business, sir.
Detective: Where were you during that hour?
Butler: In the kitchen, polishing the silver. Thursday is silver night. It has been since before you were born, I imagine.
Detective: Was anyone with you?
Butler: Only the silver, sir. Forty-two forks. They're not very talkative.
Detective: Did you hear anything? Footsteps? Doors?
Butler: Nothing at all. The kitchen is at the far end of the house. You could fire a cannon in the gallery and I wouldn't hear it.
Detective: And you didn't go upstairs at any point?
Butler: Not once. I had no reason to.
Detective: Odd. The maid says she saw a light in the gallery at about half past nine.
Butler: Then perhaps the maid should be sitting in this chair. She's been known to enjoy a glass of sherry on Thursdays.
Detective: Noted. One last thing. What did you think of the painting that was taken?
Butler: Honestly? A dreadful thing. The old lord in that ridiculous hat. And the frame was far too heavy for such a small picture.
Detective: Too heavy. Interesting.
Butler: Is it?
Detective: Lord Ashby hasn't told anyone which painting was taken. Not even the staff. There are thirty of them in that gallery.
Butler: I... may have heard the maid mention it.
Detective: The maid thinks it was a vase. And you still haven't explained how you know what the frame weighs.
Butler: Ah.
Detective: Take your time, Mr. Hale.
Butler: On second thoughts, sir, I will have that tea. I have a feeling we'll be here for a while.

title: The Village or the Cure
ru: Герой и напарница спорят: спасти деревню от пожара или успеть забрать лекарство для целого города
text:
Mira: Caden, stop. Look at the ridge. That's smoke.
Caden: I see it. It's coming from Lowbrook.
Mira: The bandits must have torched it on their way past. There are families down there.
Caden: And the bandits have the cure. If we lose their trail now, we'll never pick it up again.
Mira: You're seriously weighing medicine against children?
Caden: I'm weighing one village against a whole city. Three thousand people with the fever, Mira. That cart is carrying the last batch.
Mira: Numbers. You always hide behind numbers.
Caden: Because numbers don't change when you feel bad about them.
Mira: Neither do burnt houses.
Caden: Think about it. Why would bandits waste time setting a village on fire? They're in a hurry.
Mira: Because they're monsters?
Caden: Because they know someone's following them. They want us to stop. It's a delaying tactic.
Mira: So we just let it work? Ride past and pretend we didn't see?
Caden: I didn't say that. I said it's a trap. Knowing it's a trap doesn't make the fire any less real.
Mira: Then we split up. I go to the village, you go after the cart.
Caden: Alone? There are six of them. I'd last about a minute.
Mira: You'd last two. You're very good at running away.
Caden: Thanks for the vote of confidence.
Mira: Wait. Look at the road. The cart tracks turn off here. Towards Lowbrook. And there's a broken wheel in the ditch.
Caden: They didn't burn the village to slow us down. They burned it so nobody would notice them stealing a new wheel.
Mira: So the cure is down there too. We don't have to choose after all.
Caden: Wonderful. Now we get to do both.
Mira: You take the bandits. I'll take the buckets.
Caden: Why do I always get the bandits?
Mira: Because you're so good at running. For once, try running towards them.

title: Before the Last Fight
about: Экшен-RPG · монолог злодея и ответ героя
ru: Перед финальной битвой злодей объясняет, почему он прав, а героиня отвечает ему по-своему
text:
Veyl: So. You climbed all nine hundred steps. I'm almost flattered.
Aria: Nine hundred and twelve. I counted. You could've put in a lift.
Veyl: Lifts are for people in a hurry. I have waited four centuries for this moment. Sit, if you like.
Aria: I'll stand. Let me guess. There's a speech.
Veyl: There is an explanation. You've earned that much. Look out of the window. What do you see?
Aria: Fields. Rivers. A city that was doing fine until you turned up.
Veyl: Doing fine? I've watched that city burn six times. Every king promises peace, and every king ends up sending boys to die over a strip of mud.
Aria: So your answer is to turn everyone into your puppets.
Veyl: My answer is order. When the crown is mine, there will be no more wars, no more famine, no more choices that end in graves.
Aria: No more choices at all, you mean.
Veyl: Choice is overrated. Ask the widows what freedom bought them.
Aria: I don't need to ask. My mother was one. She hated the king, the war, the tax collectors and the weather. But every time, she chose to rebuild. Nobody made her.
Veyl: Touching. And pointless. She would have been happier under me.
Aria: Maybe. But she wouldn't have been her.
Veyl: Pretty words don't stop a blade, child.
Aria: No. But they do keep you talking.
Veyl: What is that supposed to mean?
Aria: You've been talking for ten minutes. My friend Tobin has been in your basement for nine of them.
Veyl: The basement? The basement is where I keep the—
Aria: The crystal that powers your shield. Yes. He's very good with a hammer.
Veyl: You tricked me. With conversation.
Aria: To be fair, you did most of the work. So, shall we fight? Or would you like to finish your speech first?

title: What Went Wrong
about: Командный шутер · разбор проигрыша после матча

Lee: Then we go over the bridge, and Bo runs off on his own to the tower.

Bo: Who calls it a plank?
Lee: Everyone who's ever seen a plank.
Zara: Okay, okay. Round three. The captain calls a full retreat, and then... nobody retreats. Why did nobody retreat?
Finn: What retreat? I didn't hear a retreat.
Zara: Me neither. Come to think of it, Captain, I didn't hear a single call from you all match.
Captain: That's impossible. I was talking non-stop. Those were the best calls of my life.
Lee: Check your mic settings.
Captain: My mic is... oh. It's on push-to-talk. And I never pushed.
Bo: So for forty minutes you were giving brilliant speeches to your bedroom wall.
Captain: Right. Fine. We lost as a team. But some of us lost a bit more quietly than others.

title: Salt for Silence
ru: Два правителя в пошаговой стратегии заключают хитрую сделку, и каждый пытается перехитрить другого
text:
Queen Oda: Duke Marrow. Thank you for coming. Wine?
Duke Marrow: Only if you drink first. Last turn your cavalry was camped on my border.
Queen Oda: Training exercises. Horses get bored. Now — you have salt, and I have iron. I think we can help each other.
Duke Marrow: I'm listening. Cautiously.
Queen Oda: Twenty iron every turn for the next ten turns. In return, twenty salt and an open border for my merchants.
Duke Marrow: Merchants. Is that what we're calling them now? The last merchants you sent me were carrying spears.
Queen Oda: Fine. No open border. Just salt for iron, and a promise that neither of us attacks the other for ten turns.
Duke Marrow: Why ten?
Queen Oda: Because it's a nice round number.
Duke Marrow: Nothing about you is round, Your Majesty. Everything has corners.
Queen Oda: I'll take that as a compliment. Do we have a deal or not?
Duke Marrow: Fifteen salt for twenty iron. Call it a fee for the trouble of trusting you.
Queen Oda: Eighteen. And I'll throw in the old lighthouse on the coast.
Duke Marrow: The one that's falling into the sea?
Queen Oda: It has character.
Duke Marrow: Done. Sign here. And here. And there's a little box on the back.
Queen Oda: A pleasure doing business. Safe journey home, Duke.
Pell: Your Majesty, why give that snake so much iron? He'll turn it into swords.
Queen Oda: Because my scouts say his salt mine runs dry in four turns. After that, he owes me salt he doesn't have. And a ruler who breaks a treaty loses every friend on the map.
Pell: Brilliant. So in four turns, the whole world turns against him.
Queen Oda: Exactly. By the way, what was that little box on the back of the treaty?
Pell: Let me see. It says... “All iron to be delivered in advance.”
Queen Oda: In advance? All ten turns?
Pell: Two hundred iron, Majesty. Today. I'm afraid he read the treaty more carefully than you did.

o: The Duke may attack after five turns

title: A Yellow Circle and Four Ghosts
ru: Pac-Man — простая и очень известная аркада из Японии
text:
One day in Tokyo, a young game designer was eating pizza — or so the famous story says. He took one slice and looked at the rest: a circle with one piece missing. He saw a hero.

The designer was Toru Iwatani, and Namco, a Japanese company, made his game in 1980. At that time most arcade games — big game machines in game rooms — were about space and shooting. Iwatani wanted something different: a game about eating, for everyone, not only for boys.

Pac-Man is in a maze, a place with many walls and paths. He eats small dots. When all the dots are gone, the level is finished. But four ghosts are in the maze too: red Blinky, pink Pinky, blue Inky and orange Clyde. Blinky chases you, and Pinky tries to get in front of you.

In the corners there are four big dots. When Pac-Man eats one, the ghosts turn dark blue and run away. Now Pac-Man can eat them!

In Japan the game's first name was Puck-Man, from “paku paku” — the Japanese sound of a mouth that opens and closes. In America the name became Pac-Man. Today this yellow circle is one of the most famous faces in games — and it doesn't even have a nose.

What happens after Pac-Man eats a big dot?

title: My Little Island
ru: Animal Crossing: New Horizons — спокойная игра о жизни на острове
text:
In March 2020 many people around the world could not leave their homes. And just then, Nintendo gave them a whole island.

Animal Crossing: New Horizons came out for the Nintendo Switch in March 2020. You arrive on an empty island with a tent. Your new neighbours are animals, and they can talk: a lazy cat, a sporty frog, a sweet little squirrel.

The boss of the island is Tom Nook. He looks like a raccoon, and he wears a shirt. He helps you to get a real house... and then he gives you the bill. You pay with bells, the money of the game. Players love him and make a lot of jokes about him.

What do you do all day? You catch fish and bugs. You find old bones — fossils — and give them to Blathers, an owl. He runs the island museum, but he is afraid of bugs. You plant flowers and build bridges.

The clock in the game is the real clock. When it is night in your city, it is night on the island too. In winter there is snow, and in spring the cherry trees have pink flowers.

Nobody shoots, and nobody wins. You just live, slowly. In a difficult year, that was exactly what millions of people needed.

What animal is Blathers?
What happens when it is night in your city?
o: It is night on the island too.

title: Run, Jump and Fall
ru: Fall Guys — весёлая онлайн-игра с забегами и падениями
text:
Imagine a TV game show — the kind where people in funny costumes run over giant obstacles and fall into the water. Now imagine that you are one of those people. That is Fall Guys.

The game came out in August 2020. Mediatonic, a studio in Britain, made it. Many players start a show together, and everyone is a little jelly bean with short arms and short legs. The beans are soft, round and very bad at standing up.

Every show has several rounds. In a race, you run over moving floors, jump over big turning hammers and try not to fall. In other rounds you play in teams, or you must stay on the floor when it disappears under your feet. After each round, some players go home. In the last round, only one bean wins. The prize is a golden crown.

Losing is half the fun. Your bean flies through the air, hits a wall and rolls away like a ball. You laugh, and you play again.

The costumes are a big part of the game too. Your bean can be a hot dog, a banana or a dinosaur. In 2022 Fall Guys became free, so now anyone can join. Just don't expect your bean to stay on its feet.

o: The game became a TV show.

title: Birds, Pigs and a Slingshot
ru: Angry Birds — простая игра для телефона про злых птиц и зелёных свиней
text:
Some green pigs stole the birds' eggs. Now the birds are very, very angry. And they have a slingshot.

Angry Birds came out in December 2009 on the iPhone. It came from Rovio, a small company in Finland. Before this game, Rovio made a lot of games, but not many people knew them. Angry Birds changed everything.

You play with one finger. You pull the bird back in the slingshot, choose the angle and let go. The bird flies across the screen and crashes into the pigs' buildings — made of wood, glass and stone. The walls fall down, the pigs disappear, and you get points. Easy? Not always. Sometimes you need twenty tries for the last pig.

Every bird is different. Red, the first bird, is simple and strong. The yellow bird flies very fast when you touch the screen. The blue bird turns into three small birds. The black bird is a bomb — it explodes! And when you miss, the pigs laugh at you.

The game became a huge hit. People played it on buses, in long lines at the shop and in bed at night. Then there were toys, cartoons and, in 2016, a film. Not bad for a game about birds and pigs.

title: One Hundred Players, One Island
ru: Fortnite — королевская битва со строительством, концертами и скинами
text:
A blue bus flies over a colourful island. One hundred players jump out of it, fall towards the ground and open their gliders. Nobody has a weapon yet. In a few seconds, the race begins.

This is Fortnite Battle Royale. The American company Epic Games released Fortnite in 2017. At first, it was a different game called Save the World, where friends fought zombie-like monsters together. A couple of months later, Epic added a free mode with one simple rule: the last player standing wins. That mode changed everything.

During a match, a deadly storm moves across the map, and the safe area gets smaller and smaller. Sooner or later, everyone has to meet — and fight.

What makes Fortnite different from other shooters is building. If someone shoots at you, you can build a wall, a ramp or even a tall tower in a second. Good players often build faster than they shoot. Beginners just panic.

The game is bright and silly, not dark. Players dance after a win, and there are thousands of skins — outfits for your character. You can be a banana, a superhero or a hero from Star Wars or Marvel.

Fortnite also became a place for big events. Famous musicians gave concerts inside the game, and millions of players watched together from the island.

Here is the strangest moment in its history. In 2019, at the end of a season, a black hole swallowed the whole map. For more than a day, nobody could play. They could only look at a black hole on the screen — and millions of them did. Then a brand-new island appeared.

For many people, Fortnite is not just a game. It is a place to meet friends.

o: A game where friends fought monsters together

title: A Gun That Makes Doors
ru: Portal — короткая, но гениальная головоломка от Valve
text:
You wake up in a small white room. A calm computer voice welcomes you to a test. There is no story and no explanation — just a door and, soon, a strange gun in your hands.

This is Portal, a puzzle game from Valve. It came out in 2007 as part of The Orange Box, together with Half-Life 2 and Team Fortress 2. Many people bought the box for the other games but remember Portal best.

The gun does not shoot bullets. It makes portals. You shoot a blue one on one wall and an orange one on another. Walk into the blue one, and you come out of the orange one. Simple? Then the game starts to play tricks on your mind. Put one portal on the floor and another one high on a wall, and jump in. You come out flying. The faster you fall, the faster you fly out.

You play as Chell, a woman who never says a word. The voice belongs to GLaDOS, the computer that runs the test centre of a company called Aperture Science. She is polite, funny and a little scary. She promises you cake when the tests are over. Should you believe her? Players still joke about that cake.

In one test you must carry a cube with a pink heart on it, and the game asks you to treat it like a friend. Strangely, many players felt sad when they had to say goodbye to a box.

Here is a fun fact: Portal started as a student project. A small team of students made a portal game at their college, and Valve liked it so much that it hired them.

Portal takes only a few hours to finish. But almost nobody forgets it.

title: Football With Cars
ru: Rocket League — футбол на машинах с ракетными двигателями
text:
Take football. Remove the players. Put in small cars with rocket engines, make the ball much bigger than the cars, and let them jump and fly. It sounds silly, but it is brilliant. This is Rocket League.

Rocket League comes from Psyonix, a small American studio. It came out in July 2015 on PlayStation 4 and PC. That month, PlayStation Plus members could download it for free, so millions of people tried it at once. Many never stopped.

The rules are simple. Two teams, usually of three cars, play in a closed arena with walls and a ceiling. A match lasts five minutes. Push the ball into the other team's goal. That's it.

But the cars can do amazing things. They can drive on the walls, jump twice and use boost to fly through the air. The best players hit the ball while they are flying high above the field — these shots are called aerials. When a beginner tries one, the car usually misses the ball and lands on its roof.

You can also destroy other cars. If you hit someone at full speed, their car explodes and comes back a few seconds later. Nobody gets hurt, of course.

Here is the surprise: Rocket League was not Psyonix's first try. In 2008 the studio made a very similar game for PlayStation 3 with a long, funny name: Supersonic Acrobatic Rocket-Powered Battle-Cars. It was not a big hit. Seven years later, with a shorter name and better graphics, the same idea became a hit.

In 2019 Epic Games bought the studio, and in 2020 the game became free for everyone. It is also a serious esport now.

The lesson? Sometimes a great idea just needs a second chance — and a better name.

title: Bananas on the Road
ru: Mario Kart 8 — самые весёлые гонки Nintendo
text:
You are in first place. The finish line is close. And then you hear a terrible sound behind you: a blue shell is coming. It flies over everyone and goes straight for the leader — you. Welcome to Mario Kart.

Mario Kart 8 is a racing game from Nintendo. It came out on the Wii U in 2014. Not many people owned a Wii U, so in 2017 Nintendo released Mario Kart 8 Deluxe for the Switch, with extra content and a better battle mode. This time, almost everyone played it. It became the best-selling game on the Nintendo Switch.

You race as Mario, Luigi, Princess Peach, Bowser and many other characters — even Link from The Legend of Zelda. The tracks are bright and full of jokes: a road made of rainbows, a canyon of sweets and cakes, a race through the clouds. The big new idea in this game was anti-gravity. On some parts of a track, your wheels turn sideways, and you drive along walls or even upside down.

But the real fun is the items. You drop bananas behind you and shoot green and red shells at other drivers. A mushroom gives you a short burst of speed. The game is fair in a funny way: players at the back get better items than players at the front. So a bad driver can still win, and a great one can lose in the last second.

That is why Mario Kart is perfect for parties. Even beginners can play, because the game can help them steer and keep the speed up.

In 2022 and 2023, Nintendo added 48 more tracks, most of them old favourites from earlier games, so now there are 96. Ten years after the first version, people were still buying it.

title: The Game That Made Fighting Games Popular
ru: Street Fighter II — легендарный файтинг, с которого начался бум жанра
text:
In 1991, if you walked into an arcade, you saw a crowd around one machine. Some people were playing, others were watching, and some left a coin on the machine. That coin meant “I'm next.” The game was Street Fighter II.

The first Street Fighter by the Japanese company Capcom came out in 1987, but few people remember it. The second one was a huge hit. It offered eight fighters from around the world, and each one felt completely different.

Ryu and Ken are karate fighters who can throw fireballs. Chun-Li, a police officer from China, has very fast kicks, and she was one of the first women you could play in a fighting game. Guile is an American air force officer with a very tall haircut. Blanka is a green wild man from Brazil who can shoot electricity. Dhalsim from India can stretch his arms and legs across the screen. And there is Zangief, a huge Russian wrestler who loves to spin and grab people.

At first, the special moves felt like a secret. You had to move the joystick in a certain way and press a button at the right moment. Kids shared these tricks at school like magic spells.

Here is a famous fact: combos — chains of hits that the other player cannot stop — started as an accident. The developers noticed that some attacks could connect very quickly. They decided this “bug” was fun and kept it. Today, combos are a basic part of almost every fighting game.

After that, Capcom released new version after new version: Champion Edition, Turbo, Super, Super Turbo. Fans still joke about it, but people bought every one.

Many famous fighting games came later, and almost all of them learned something from this one.

Where is Zangief from?

o: As an accident that the developers kept
