title: Dig, Build and Fight
ru: Terraria — двухмерная песочница, где копают, строят и сражаются с боссами
text:
At first, Terraria looks like a simple 2D game. You have a small pickaxe, some trees and a little house to build before night. Then the sun goes down, zombies start knocking on your door, and a giant flying eye appears in the sky.

Terraria came out in 2011. A small American studio called Re-Logic made it. Many people called it “2D Minecraft”, because you dig, collect blocks and build. But Terraria is much more about adventure. Under your feet there is a huge world: caves, jungles, underground lakes and, at the very bottom, the Underworld — a land of fire and lava.

The game is famous for its bosses. Some of them come when you use a special item. Others just arrive when they want. Each boss is harder than the one before, and each one gives you better weapons and armour. There are thousands of items in the game: swords, guns, magic books, wings and even a sword that makes stars fall from the sky.

Your world slowly fills with people. If you build a good house with a door, a table, a chair and a light, a new character will come and live there. The Guide gives advice, the Merchant sells things, and the Nurse heals you — for money, of course.

Here is a funny story. In 2020 the developers released an update called Journey's End and said it was the last big one. Then they made another update. And another. Now fans laugh every time Re-Logic calls something “the final update”.

You can play alone or with friends, and the game never really ends. That's why some players spend more than a thousand hours in it — and still find secrets.

title: Go Anywhere, Climb Everything
about: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild (2017)
wiki: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild
ru: Zelda: Breath of the Wild — открытый мир, где можно залезть на любую гору
text:
Imagine a game that shows you a mountain far away and says: “Yes, you can go there.” That is the big promise of The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild. Nintendo released it in 2017 on the brand-new Nintendo Switch and on the older Wii U.

You play as Link. He wakes up in a cave after sleeping for one hundred years, and he doesn't remember anything. Outside, the kingdom of Hyrule is green, beautiful and almost empty. Many old towns are ruins now, with only broken walls left. A dark power called Calamity Ganon is waiting in Hyrule Castle, and Princess Zelda is trying to hold it back.

The best thing about the game is freedom. Link can climb almost any wall, tree or cliff, but he gets tired, so you must watch his stamina, his energy for climbing and running. From the top of a hill, he can jump and fly down with a paraglider. You can even go straight to the final boss at the start. It's a terrible idea, but the game lets you try!

The world feels alive. When it rains, rocks get wet and Link slips down. In a storm, lightning can hit you if you are carrying metal weapons. And swords break all the time, so you always have to look for new ones.

There are also 120 shrines, small rooms with clever puzzles, and hundreds of tiny forest creatures called Koroks, who hide under rocks and on top of trees.

Players loved it, and it won Game of the Year at The Game Awards. In 2023 the sequel arrived: Tears of the Kingdom.

title: Sunflowers Against the Undead
ru: Plants vs. Zombies — забавная стратегия, где растения защищают дом от зомби
text:
Zombies are coming to your house. What do you use to stop them? Soldiers? Tanks? No — sunflowers and peas.

Plants vs. Zombies came out in 2009. It was made by PopCap Games, an American studio, and its main designer was George Fan. The idea sounds silly, but the game is surprisingly clever.

In front of your house there is a lawn, an area of short grass, and the zombies walk slowly across it from the right side of the screen. You put plants in the rows to stop them. The Peashooter shoots green peas. The Wall-nut is a big, tough nut that the zombies have to chew through, and while they are chewing, your other plants keep shooting. The Cherry Bomb simply explodes. But the most important plant is the smiling Sunflower. It makes sun, and sun is the money of the game. No sunflowers, no army.

The zombies are funny too. One wears a traffic cone on his head, and another wears a metal bucket, so they are harder to kill. One zombie walks along reading a newspaper, and he gets very angry when you destroy it. Later levels happen at night, in a swimming pool and on a roof, and every place needs different plants.

Your guide is your neighbor, Crazy Dave. He talks nonsense, sells you new plants and wears a cooking pot on his head.

If a zombie gets into your house, it eats your brains and you lose. But on the lawn each row has an old lawnmower, your last chance to save the day.

The game was a huge hit on computers and later on phones, and a sequel came out in 2013.

title: Counter-Strike: From a Mod to a Legend
ru: Counter-Strike — как фанатский мод стал одним из главных шутеров в мире
text:
Some of the biggest games in the world were made by huge companies with huge budgets. Counter-Strike was made by two fans in their free time.

In 1999, Minh Le and Jess Cliffe released a mod (a free, fan-made modification) for the shooter Half-Life. Their idea was simple. Two teams, terrorists and counter-terrorists, fight on a small map. The terrorists try to plant a bomb or guard hostages, and the counter-terrorists try to stop them. The mod spread through internet cafés and university networks so fast that Valve, the company behind Half-Life, hired the creators and released Counter-Strike as an official game in 2000.

What made it different? First, it is round-based. If you die, you don't come back after three seconds. You sit and watch your teammates until the round ends, and that makes every life valuable. Second, there is an economy. At the start of each round, players buy weapons and armour with money they earned in the previous rounds. Sometimes a team decides to save money and lose a round on purpose, so that it can afford better guns later. Counter-Strike rewards patience, aim and teamwork more than running around.

Some of its maps have become legends. Dust II, a sandy town with narrow streets and long corridors, has been played so often that many players can walk through it with their eyes closed. Every corner has a name, and players use these names to communicate quickly: “two at B, one long”.

Over the years, the series has changed its look several times: Counter-Strike: Source in 2004, Global Offensive in 2012, and Counter-Strike 2 in 2023, which replaced Global Offensive completely. Global Offensive also became famous for its weapon skins, decorative designs that players buy, sell and trade, some of them for surprisingly large amounts of real money. In 2018 it became free to play.

Today, Counter-Strike is also one of the most important esports. Its biggest tournaments are called Majors, and they fill arenas with thousands of fans. Not bad for a project that two fans started for fun.

o: As a mod for Half-Life made by fans

title: Civilization: History in Your Hands
ru: Civilization — пошаговая стратегия, где ведёшь народ от каменного века к космосу
text:
There is a famous joke among strategy fans: “Just one more turn.” You say it at ten in the evening. Then you say it again at midnight. Then you look out of the window and see that the sun is rising. The game that made this joke famous is Sid Meier's Civilization.

The first Civilization was released in 1991 by the American designer Sid Meier and the company MicroProse. The idea was enormous for its time. You start with a group of settlers in 4000 BC and lead your people through the whole of human history. You build cities, discover writing, farming and gunpowder, make friends and enemies with other nations, and finally reach the space age. In the first game, one way to win was to build a spaceship and send it to the star Alpha Centauri.

Civilization is turn-based, which means nothing happens while you think. You make your moves, the computer makes its moves, and then the next turn begins. This is exactly why it is so hard to stop: every turn brings something new, like a finished building, a new invention or an angry neighbour on your border.

The series became one of the most respected in gaming. Since the third game, it has been made by Firaxis, a studio Sid Meier co-founded, and new parts keep coming: Civilization VI in 2016 and Civilization VII in 2025. Each part has changed the rules, but the heart of the game is the same.

Here is a surprise: Civilization IV made history outside games, too. Its opening song, “Baba Yetu” by Christopher Tin, a version of the Lord's Prayer in Swahili, became the first piece of video game music to win a Grammy award.

And then there is Gandhi. For years, the internet told a story that a bug in the first game made peaceful Gandhi extremely aggressive and keen on nuclear weapons. Sid Meier has said that this bug never existed. However, the developers loved the legend so much that in later games they made Gandhi a fan of nuclear weapons on purpose.

For a language learner, Civilization is a treasure. Every invention comes with a short text, so you learn history and English at the same time, one more turn at a time.

title: Resident Evil: The Mansion Where Horror Began
ru: Resident Evil — серия, которая сделала «survival horror» популярным жанром
text:
A team of special police officers runs into an old mansion in the forest to escape from a pack of monstrous dogs. The doors close behind them. The house is silent, beautiful and full of secrets. In a dark corridor, a man is kneeling over a body. Slowly, he turns his head towards you, and his face is not human anymore.

This is the opening of Resident Evil, released by the Japanese company Capcom in 1996 for the first PlayStation. In Japan it is called Biohazard. Its director, Shinji Mikami, wanted to create a game that felt like a horror film, and he succeeded so well that the game helped to make a whole genre popular: survival horror.

You play as Chris Redfield or Jill Valentine, members of the S.T.A.R.S. police team, who are investigating strange murders near Raccoon City. Inside the Spencer Mansion they find zombies, giant snakes and laboratories, and slowly they discover that a powerful company called Umbrella has been doing terrible experiments with a virus.

What made the game so scary was not only the monsters. It was the feeling of being weak. Bullets are rare, so you often have to decide whether to fight or run. The camera is fixed in the corners of rooms, like a security camera, so you often hear an enemy before you can see it. Even saving your progress costs something: you can only save at typewriters, and only if you have found an ink ribbon. Players still remember the moment when dogs suddenly jumped through a window in a quiet corridor.

Funnily enough, the English voice acting in the original version was so awkward that some of its lines became internet jokes. Fans love it anyway.

Since then, Resident Evil has changed many times. Resident Evil 4 in 2005 moved the camera behind the hero's shoulder and influenced many action games. Resident Evil 7 in 2017 went back to pure horror with a first-person view. Capcom has also remade the old games with modern graphics, and the series inspired a long line of Hollywood films starring Milla Jovovich.

Thirty years later, the mansion's doors are still open, and players still walk in nervously.

title: Undertale: Mercy Instead of Fighting
ru: Undertale — инди-RPG одного автора, где врагов можно пощадить
text:
In most role-playing games, a monster appears and you attack it. In Undertale, a monster appears and you can ask it about its day, tell it a joke, give it a compliment, or simply let it go. You can finish the whole game without killing anyone. And the game remembers everything you do.

Undertale was released in 2015 by Toby Fox, an American developer who made it almost completely alone. He wrote the story, designed the game and composed all of the music. He raised money for it on Kickstarter, and the result became one of the most loved indie games of its decade, even though it looks like something from the early 1990s.

The story begins when a human child falls into the Underground, a world under a mountain where monsters have lived since they lost a war against humans long ago. Every monster you meet has a personality of its own. There is Toriel, a kind goat-like woman who looks after you like a mother. There are two skeleton brothers: Papyrus, who loves puzzles and dreams of capturing a human to become famous, and Sans, a lazy joker who seems to know much more than he says.

The battles are unusual, too. When an enemy attacks, your soul, a small red heart, appears in a box, and you must move it to avoid bullets, bones and other objects. Each monster attacks in its own way, so each fight feels like a small puzzle. If you choose mercy, you have to understand what the monster needs before you can spare it.

The most surprising thing about Undertale is how it plays with the player. If you load an old save to undo a bad decision, some characters may notice. They talk to you, not only to the child on the screen. This makes your choices feel heavy, and many players have changed the way they play because they did not want to hurt anyone.

The game's music, especially the intense track “Megalovania”, became famous far beyond the game. Toby Fox later started a new project in a similar world, called Deltarune.

Undertale is short, funny and strange, and it asks a simple question: do you really have to fight?

title: Is Esports a Real Sport?
about: Esports (about games): League of Legends, Counter-Strike and others
ru: Про игры: киберспорт — стадионы, команды, тренировки и спор о том, спорт ли это
text:
In the Polish city of Katowice there is an arena that looks like a flying saucer. It is called the Spodek, which means “saucer” in Polish. Almost every year it fills with thousands of screaming fans, flags and cameras, but they have not come to see a band or a basketball match. They have come to watch people play Counter-Strike. Welcome to esports.

Twenty-five years ago, playing video games for money sounded like a joke. Today, the best players train like athletes and compete for prizes that can reach millions of dollars. The most popular esports are team games such as League of Legends, Counter-Strike and Dota 2, but there are serious tournaments for fighting games, football games, racing games and even Tetris.

The stars are real stars. Lee Sang-hyeok, known as Faker, has won the League of Legends World Championship several times, and in South Korea he is treated like a famous footballer. Big matches are shown on huge screens, explained by commentators and watched online by millions of people.

Behind the show there is a lot of hard work. Professional players belong to clubs, just like footballers. They have coaches, analysts and sometimes psychologists, and many of them practise for ten hours a day or more. Careers are short: many players retire before thirty, because younger players often react faster.

So, is it a real sport? People who say no point out that players don't run, jump or lift anything. People who say yes reply that chess is often called a sport, too, and that esports demands speed, strategy, teamwork and strong nerves under pressure. Imagine making a decision in half a second while a whole stadium is watching you. In 2023, esports was included as a medal event at the Asian Games, which gave the second side a strong argument.

Whatever you decide, esports is a great tool for learning English. Most international tournaments are broadcast in English, and the commentators speak fast, clearly and with a lot of emotion. If you watch a match of a game you know well, you will be surprised how much you understand, and you will soon start shouting “What a play!” at your screen.

title: Can Video Games Teach You English?
ru: Про игры: как с помощью видеоигр учить английский и что для этого лучше подходит
text:
Ask a group of people who speak good English how they learned it, and you will often hear a surprising answer: “Not at school. From games.” It sounds like an excuse to play more, but there is real logic behind it.

The secret is motivation. When you read a grammar book, nothing happens if you don't understand a sentence. In a game, it matters. If you don't understand the quest, you get lost. If you misread the instructions, your character dies. Your brain decides that these words are important, and it remembers them much better.

Games also repeat language naturally. In a role-playing game you will see words like “quest”, “reward”, “inventory” and “armour” hundreds of times, always in context. You don't need to memorise them. One day you simply realise that you know them.

However, not every game is equally useful. A fast shooter where nobody talks will teach you very little. The best games for learning are the ones with a lot of story and text: role-playing games, adventure games, detective games and visual novels, which are like interactive books. Games with good voice acting and subtitles are even better, because you can read and listen at the same time. Slow games are best, because you can stop and think whenever you want.

Here are some tips if you want to try it:

First, switch the whole game to English, including the menus. It will feel strange for a day or two, then it will feel normal.

Second, choose a game you have already played in your own language. You know the story, so you can guess the meaning of new words more easily.

Third, keep a notebook or a phone app nearby, but don't stop every ten seconds. Write down only the words that appear again and again, or the phrases you like.

Finally, try to use the language, not only receive it. Online co-op games and fan forums are full of people from different countries who use English to communicate. Even a short message like “Need help with this boss?” is real practice.

Games will not replace everything. You still need some grammar and a bit of patience. But if you are going to play anyway, why not let your favourite hobby work for you?

title: How Game Music Is Made
about: Video game soundtracks (about games): Koji Kondo, Nobuo Uematsu, C418, Mick Gordon
ru: Про игры: как пишут музыку для игр — от 8-битных мелодий до адаптивных саундтреков
text:
Hum the theme from Super Mario Bros. Chances are you can do it without thinking, even if you have not played the game in years. That tune was written by Koji Kondo for Nintendo in 1985, and it was squeezed out of a machine that could produce only a handful of sounds at the same time.

Early game composers worked under brutal technical limits. The Nintendo Entertainment System had just five sound channels: two for melody, one usually used for bass, one for noise and one for very short recorded samples. There was no orchestra, no singer, no echo. Kondo had to write music catchy enough to survive being looped for hours, and he wanted it to match the bouncy rhythm of a plumber running and jumping, so that it felt like part of the action rather than background noise.

As hardware improved, composers gained room to dream. Nobuo Uematsu's scores for the Final Fantasy series turned simple chip tunes into sweeping, emotional music, and by Final Fantasy VII in 1997 one of his battle themes even featured choir voices chanting in Latin. Today his music is performed by real orchestras in concert halls around the world, for audiences who often cheer when they recognize the first few notes.

Not all great game music is big and dramatic, though. When Daniel Rosenfeld, better known as C418, wrote the soundtrack for Minecraft, he chose quiet, gentle piano pieces that play only now and then. The effect is strangely moving: you are building a house alone in a huge blocky world, the sun is setting, and a few soft notes drift in out of nowhere. For millions of players, that music now sounds like childhood.

At the opposite extreme is Mick Gordon's soundtrack for Doom (2016). Instead of a traditional orchestra, he built a wall of distorted synthesizers and heavy guitars, including nine-string models tuned extremely low. The music is aggressive by design. It is there to push you forward and make you feel that hesitating is a mistake.

What makes game music truly different from film music is that the composer cannot know exactly what will happen on screen. A film scene always lasts the same number of seconds; a battle in a game might take ten seconds or ten minutes. That is why modern games often use adaptive music — soundtracks built in layers that change according to what the player does. Walk calmly through a forest, and you might hear soft strings. Draw your sword, and drums join in. Win the fight, and the music relaxes again, often without you noticing the switch.

The best game composers, then, are not only musicians but also designers. Their job is to write music that bends to the player while still sounding like a finished piece. When it works, you barely notice it at all — until, years later, you catch yourself humming it in the shower.

title: Last One Standing: The Rise of Battle Royale
about: The battle royale genre (about games): DayZ mods, PUBG, Fortnite, Apex Legends, Warzone
ru: Про игры: откуда взялся жанр королевской битвы и почему он захватил мир
text:
A hundred strangers jump out of a plane over an island. They land with nothing, scramble for weapons and supplies, and try to survive while the safe area keeps shrinking. Only one player or team will be left at the end. Described like that, battle royale sounds like a nightmare. In practice, it became one of the most popular game genres ever made.

The name comes from Battle Royale, a 2000 Japanese film based on a novel by Koushun Takami, in which a class of schoolchildren is forced to fight on an island until only one remains. The idea of a last-person-standing contest was hardly new, but the title stuck, and gamers borrowed it.

The genre's real father is Brendan Greene, an Irish developer better known by his online name, PlayerUnknown. In the early 2010s he created battle royale mods — fan-made modifications — for the military simulator Arma 2, building on the popular zombie mod DayZ, and later for Arma 3. His rules became the template: random loot, a huge map and a deadly zone that forces players closer and closer together.

In 2017 Greene's ideas grew into a full game, PlayerUnknown's Battlegrounds, or PUBG. Even in early access, while it was officially unfinished, it attracted enormous numbers of players and dominated streaming sites. Its cheerful victory message, which promised the winner a chicken dinner, became a meme.

Then Epic Games moved fast. Fortnite had launched as a co-operative mode about fighting zombie-like creatures, but in September 2017 Epic added a free battle royale mode. It had bright cartoon graphics, silly dances and one unique twist: players could build walls, ramps and towers in seconds. Because it was free to play, it reached a vast young audience, and Fortnite soon became a cultural phenomenon, hosting live concerts and in-game events watched by millions.

Other studios followed. In 2019 Respawn Entertainment surprised everyone by releasing Apex Legends with almost no advance marketing. It focused on small squads of characters with special abilities and introduced a clever “ping” system, which let teammates mark enemies and items without saying a word. In 2020 Call of Duty: Warzone brought the genre to one of gaming's biggest series, adding a second-chance arena called the Gulag, where eliminated players could fight their way back into the match.

Why does the formula work so well? Every match tells a new story. You might win with a perfect strategy or by hiding in a bush for twenty minutes. The shrinking zone guarantees tension, and the sheer number of players means that even reaching the final ten feels like an achievement. Losing is quick, and the next match is only a click away.

Above all, battle royale is built to be watched. A close final circle, with three players left and nowhere to hide, is as dramatic as any sports final. That is why the genre conquered streaming platforms as quickly as it conquered our evenings.

title: Outer Wilds: A Solar System in Twenty-Two Minutes
ru: Outer Wilds — космическая головоломка, где единственный прогресс — это знания
text:
Most games make you stronger as you play. You collect better weapons, earn experience points and unlock new abilities. Outer Wilds, released in 2019 by the small American studio Mobius Digital and published by Annapurna Interactive, gives you none of that. From the first minute to the last, you have the same ship, the same tools and the same modest oxygen supply. The only thing that grows is what you know.

You play a young astronaut from Timber Hearth, a small forested planet whose cheerful, four-eyed inhabitants have only recently started exploring space. Their spaceship is made largely of wood, their space program has a campfire at its center, and before your first launch you can sit down and roast a marshmallow. It is one of the coziest openings in gaming — until, about twenty-two minutes later, the sun explodes.

And then you wake up by the campfire again.

You are trapped in a time loop, and every loop lasts exactly twenty-two minutes. Nothing you physically do carries over: doors you opened are closed again, and objects you moved are back where they were. What does carry over is your ship's log, where every clue you have found is recorded, and, of course, your own memory. Progress in Outer Wilds happens in the player's head.

The solar system is small enough to cross in minutes, but every planet is a strange, handmade puzzle that changes over time. On the Hourglass Twins, sand slowly pours from one planet to the other, burying some places and revealing others as the loop goes on. Brittle Hollow is a crumbling shell with a black hole at its core, and its surface falls away piece by piece. Giant's Deep is a planet-wide ocean where tornadoes hurl whole islands into the sky. Each world hides writings left by the Nomai, an ancient race who visited the system long ago, and slowly their story begins to come together.

The game began as Alex Beachum's student thesis project at the University of Southern California before Mobius Digital developed it into a full release. That origin shows in its confidence: Outer Wilds trusts its players completely. There are no quest markers and very few instructions. You simply follow your curiosity, and the game rewards you with discoveries that genuinely feel like your own.

There is also a quiet sadness running beneath the jokes. Scattered across the system are other travelers, each playing a different instrument, and you can tune a device called a signalscope to hear them from far away. As you fly, a banjo, a harmonica and a flute drift across space — a small, warm sound in the dark.

The strangest thing about Outer Wilds is that it can only truly be played once. When you know its secrets, the mystery is gone. That is why fans are so protective of it, and why the best advice anyone can give you is this: look nothing up, and go.

title: StarCraft: The Game That Built Esports in Korea
ru: StarCraft — стратегия в реальном времени, ставшая национальным спортом Южной Кореи
text:
In most countries, being a professional video game player once sounded like a joke. In South Korea at the start of the 2000s, it could make you a celebrity with your face on billboards. The game responsible was StarCraft, a science-fiction strategy game released by Blizzard Entertainment in 1998.

StarCraft is a real-time strategy game, which means nobody takes turns. You gather resources, build a base, produce an army and fight your opponent all at once, with the clock always running. The game offers three very different races. The Terrans are human exiles with tanks, marines and buildings that can lift off and fly. The Zerg are a swarm of insect-like creatures whose bases spread like living tissue and who win through sheer numbers. The Protoss are an ancient psychic species with powerful but expensive units. Balancing three completely different sides was a remarkable achievement, and players argued for years about which race was strongest — usually a sign that none of them was.

StarCraft arrived in Korea at the perfect moment. After the Asian financial crisis of 1997, the government invested heavily in fast internet, and a wave of internet cafés called PC bangs opened across the country. They were cheap places to spend an evening with friends, and the game everyone was playing was StarCraft, usually with its 1998 expansion, Brood War.

Soon cable TV channels were broadcasting matches, complete with excited commentators, studio audiences and dramatic camera work. Major companies sponsored professional teams, whose players lived together in team houses and practiced for many hours a day. Stars like Lim Yo-hwan, known as BoxeR, built huge fan bases, and the biggest finals drew crowds that many football clubs would envy.

What made StarCraft so watchable? Speed and skill. Top players perform hundreds of actions per minute, a statistic known as APM, controlling several groups of units in different places while managing their economy back home. A single mistake, such as a group of units left in the wrong spot for a few seconds, can decide a match. For viewers who understood the game, it was as tense as any traditional sport.

StarCraft II arrived in 2010, starting with Wings of Liberty. It brought modern graphics and online features, and it became one of the most important esports in the world, with major tournaments in Europe and North America as well as Korea. Korean players, however, kept dominating for years, a legacy of the system built around the original game.

Today StarCraft is no longer the giant it once was, and newer games attract bigger audiences. But almost every modern esport, with its team houses, live broadcasts and professional coaches, follows a model that Korea built around a game about humans, aliens and insects fighting over crystals.

title: Who Took the Pie?
ru: Юный детектив расспрашивает пекаря и его помощника о пропавшем пироге
text:
Detective: Good morning. I'm Detective Pip. I heard a pie went missing.

Detective: When did you last see it?
Baker: At eight o'clock. I put it by the window to cool. Then I went out for milk.
Detective: Who was in the shop?
Baker: Only Finn, my helper. Finn! Come here!
Finn: Yes, sir? Oh. Hello.
Detective: Finn, where were you at eight o'clock?

Detective: Your hands are very clean. But your shirt isn't. Is that a red spot?

Baker: Finn! Did you eat the king's pie?
Finn: No! I only tried one little piece! Then a dog jumped in through the window and took the rest!
Detective: A dog. That's an interesting story. Where is this dog now?
Finn: Under your chair, Detective. He's licking your shoes.

title: Where Is My Dragon?

title: Light Through the Mirrors
ru: Два игрока в разных комнатах башни поворачивают зеркала, чтобы луч света открыл дверь
text:
Ivy: Omar, can you hear me? I'm in a room with a huge lamp and three mirrors. Where are you?
Omar: Somewhere above you, I think. There's a hole in my floor, and light is coming through it.
Ivy: That's my lamp! The light goes up through the ceiling to your room. What happens to it there?
Omar: It hits a mirror and bounces into the wall. On the other side there's a door with a little glass eye in it.
Ivy: Then the light has to reach the eye. That's what opens the door.
Omar: Makes sense. I'll turn my mirror. Which way?
Ivy: I don't know, I can't see your room! Try turning it to the left.
Omar: My left or your left? We aren't even facing the same way.
Ivy: Okay, forget left. Turn it towards the door.
Omar: Done. Now the light's hitting the door frame. Close, but not close enough.
Ivy: Hold on. If I turn my first mirror a little, the beam will move too. Tell me when it looks right.
Omar: Keep going... keep going... stop! It's on the glass eye!
Ivy: And? Is the door opening?
Omar: No. The eye has turned red. There's writing under it: only blue light may pass.
Ivy: Blue? My lamp is yellow. Wait, there's a blue glass bottle on the shelf here.
Omar: Put it in front of the lamp. It's worth a try.
Ivy: All right... how about now?
Omar: It's blue! The eye's turning blue... the door's open! I can see some stairs.
Ivy: Brilliant. So what's at the top of the stairs?
Omar: Another room. With a lamp. And about twenty mirrors.
Ivy: You know what? Let's swap. You can do the next one.

title: The Museum Job

Nick: The Blue Lady? Is that a painting or a person?
Sid: A painting. Seventeenth century. Worth more than this whole city.
Vera: Sid cuts the power at exactly midnight. After that, we've got ninety seconds before the backup generator starts.
Nick: Ninety seconds isn't very long. What happens after that?
Sid: The lasers come back on, the doors lock, and we spend the next ten years in prison.
Nick: Great. Love that. Next question: how do we get in?
Vera: Through the roof. There's a glass window above the main hall. I'll lower you down on a rope.
Nick: Me? Why me? I've only been on the team for two days.
Vera: Because you're the lightest. And because you ask so many questions.
Sid: The guards change shifts at midnight. For a few minutes, nobody is watching the cameras.
Nick: Hold on. Have either of you actually been inside the museum?
Vera: Of course not. We've studied the plans. If you visit a museum before you rob it, people remember your face.
Nick: So how do you know the painting is still in the main hall?
Sid: Because it's always been in the main hall.

Nick: No, but there's a front door. And it's open until eleven. You can just walk in and order soup.
Sid: He's been here two days, and he's already better at this than us.
Vera: Fine. New plan. Nick, you're in charge. And you're paying for the soup.

title: The Mayor Has Questions
ru: Советник докладывает мэру о проблемах города, которые мэр сам и создал
text:
Mayor: Good morning, Graves. I've got my coffee, so give me the news. How's my beautiful city?
Advisor: Well, Mayor, people aren't very happy. Traffic is terrible all over the east side.
Mayor: Terrible? Why? Who designed those roads?
Advisor: You did, sir. Last week you replaced every road in the east with one giant roundabout.
Mayor: Ah. But it looked so nice from above. Like a flower.
Advisor: It does. Unfortunately, nobody can get out of it. One bus has been going round for six days.
Mayor: Fine. Next problem.
Advisor: Pollution. The air in the north has turned slightly brown.
Mayor: Brown? Who put a factory next to all those houses?
Advisor: Also you, sir. You said the workers would save time if they lived next door.
Mayor: And did they?
Advisor: Yes, but now they cough a lot. They've also started a protest outside the town hall.
Mayor: A protest? What do they want?
Advisor: Mostly, sir, they want a new mayor.
Mayor: That's a bit dramatic. What about money? Have we got enough to fix all this?
Advisor: We had some money. However, you spent most of it on the golden statue in the main square.
Mayor: The statue of me? But that statue is a symbol of the city's success!
Advisor: The pigeons seem to agree. They've been sitting on its head all week.
Mayor: All right, Graves, I've got an idea. If we raise taxes a little, we can afford everything.
Advisor: Sir, if we raise taxes, the people who haven't left yet will leave.
Mayor: Good point. In that case, let's build a second statue. A happier one.

title: The Legend of the Lake

June: Who's Big Martha?

Rafe: As long as a boat? Come on. That's just a story for tourists.

title: I Swear It Was My Cat
ru: Игрок звонит в поддержку, чтобы оспорить бан за «подозрительную активность»
text:
Agent: Player support, this is Dana. How can I help?
Marcus: Hi, Dana. I've been banned for three days, and I genuinely have no idea why.
Agent: Sorry to hear that. Can I take your username?
Marcus: QuietStorm. Though I'm not feeling very quiet right now.
Agent: Got it. Okay, the system flagged your account for automated play. Basically, it thinks you were using a bot.
Marcus: A bot? I've never used a bot in my life. I can barely work a microwave.
Agent: According to the logs, on Saturday night your character walked in a perfect circle around the Mossy Inn for nine hours straight.
Marcus: Nine hours? Oh no.
Agent: That's the kind of thing bots do. Real players get bored after about ten minutes.
Marcus: Right. Okay. This is going to sound ridiculous, but hear me out. I think it was my cat.
Agent: Your cat.
Marcus: Her name's Biscuit. She sleeps on my keyboard because it's warm, and I left the game running when I went to bed.
Agent: Sir, I've heard “my little brother did it” about four hundred times. The cat is a new one.
Marcus: I swear it's true! She lies across the W and the A keys. That's forward and turn left. That's a circle!
Agent: Huh. That would actually make a circle.
Marcus: I can send you a photo. I've got about two thousand photos of her lying on that keyboard.
Agent: Go ahead, there's an upload button in your ticket... okay, it's come through. Wow. She's very... orange.
Marcus: She's a big girl.
Agent: Alright, Marcus. I'm lifting the ban now, and I'll add a note to your account so it doesn't happen again.
Marcus: Dana, you're a legend. Thank you.
Agent: One more thing. During those nine hours, your character unlocked two achievements: Marathon Runner and Going in Circles.
Marcus: Seriously? I've been trying to get Marathon Runner for months.
Agent: Between you and me, Biscuit had a better weekend in this game than most of our players. Maybe let her keep the keyboard.

title: Three Suspects and a Clock
about: Детективный квест · допрос в старинном поместье
ru: Сыщица по очереди расспрашивает дворецкого, садовника и племянницу о пропаже фамильного бриллианта
text:
Inspector Crane: Thank you all for staying. As you know, the Blackwood diamond vanished from the study last night, some time after ten.
Butler: A dreadful business, Inspector. In forty years of service, nothing has ever gone missing. Apart from the occasional spoon.
Inspector Crane: Then let's start with you. Where were you between ten and eleven?
Butler: Locking up, as always. The front door at ten, the windows at half past, and the cellar at a quarter to eleven.
Inspector Crane: Did you pass the study?
Butler: Twice. The door was closed both times. I assumed the diamond was asleep, like everyone sensible.
Inspector Crane: Thank you. Mr. Dobbs, you're the gardener. What were you doing in the house at that hour?
Gardener: I wasn't. I was in the greenhouse. There was a frost coming, and my orchids hate the cold even more than I do.
Inspector Crane: Can anyone confirm that?
Gardener: The orchids could, if they talked. Look, I've got mud on my boots and I can't feel my fingers. Do I look like a man who's been creeping round a study?
Inspector Crane: Not particularly. Miss Blackwood, you're the owner's niece. Where were you?
Niece: In the library, reading. I left at eleven exactly. I remember, because I heard the study clock strike. The diamond was still there then. I saw it through the door.
Inspector Crane: The clock struck eleven. You're sure?
Niece: Completely. Eleven loud chimes. Nobody could sleep through that thing.
Gardener: Funny. That clock hasn't chimed since March.
Niece: What?
Gardener: Your aunt said it gave her headaches. Asked me to take the bell out. It's in my shed with the rakes.
Butler: He's quite right, Inspector. The house has been blissfully quiet ever since.
Inspector Crane: So you heard a clock that can't chime, Miss Blackwood. Would you like to try that story again?
Niece: Fine. I took it. But only to get it valued. I'm not a thief. I was just... curious about my inheritance.
Inspector Crane: And what did the jeweller say?
Niece: That's the awful part. It's glass. Grandfather sold the real one in 1991 to pay for the roof.
Butler: I could have told you that, miss. Who do you think arranged the sale?

title: An Offer You Can Refuse

text:
Rook: Hey, Wren, right? Got a minute? I've been looking at your healing numbers from last night's raid.
Wren: Have you, now. That's not creepy at all.
Rook: They're off the charts. Top one percent on the server. For a guild nobody's heard of, that's impressive.
Wren: We've heard of us. Who's asking?
Rook: Rook. Main tank and recruitment officer for Crimson Vanguard. Third on the server, and aiming for first.
Wren: Oh, I know who you are. Your lot camped our herb-gathering spot for six hours in May. For fun.
Rook: Water under the bridge. Look, I'll cut to the chase. We've got a spot for a main healer. Starts Friday.
Wren: I've already got a guild. The Soggy Biscuits.
Rook: The Soggy Biscuits. Right. And how far have the Soggy Biscuits got in the new raid?
Wren: Second boss. We wiped thirty times on him on Tuesday because Pete's internet kept dropping.
Rook: We cleared the whole raid in the first week. You'd get the best gear in the game. Priority loot. A guaranteed spot every night.
Wren: What's the schedule?
Rook: Four nights a week, seven till midnight. Attendance is compulsory. Miss two raids and you're out.
Wren: Wow. That sounds less like a guild and more like a second job.
Rook: That's what winning looks like.
Wren: Can I ask why the spot's opening up? What happened to your last healer?
Rook: She burned out. Left without warning. It happens.
Wren: Was her name Lark, by any chance?
Rook: How do you know that?

Rook: She what?

Rook: Hang on. Are you trying to recruit me?
Wren: Think about it. We could really use a tank who knows how to beat the second boss.

title: Let's Talk Terms, Dark Lord
about: Экшен-RPG · переговоры с боссом в его замке
ru: Вместо битвы героиня решает договориться с тёмным властелином — и находит его слабое место
text:
Lord Malgrin: So. You've reached my throne room at last. I confess, I expected someone taller.
Asha: And I expected fewer candles. Honestly, how much do you spend on these a month?
Lord Malgrin: Silence! For a thousand years I have ruled these lands. Kings have trembled before me. Heroes have—
Asha: —crumbled to dust, yes, it's on the sign by the drawbridge. Can we skip to the part where we talk?
Lord Malgrin: Talk? Heroes don't talk. Heroes draw their swords and shout something about destiny.
Asha: My sword's a bit blunt, to be honest. And I've had a long week. What do you actually want?
Lord Malgrin: What do I want? I want your kingdom on its knees. I want eternal darkness. I want... why are you looking at my desk?
Asha: Because there's a brochure on it. “Sunny Cove Cottages. Sea views. Peace and quiet.”
Lord Malgrin: That's research. Evil research.
Asha: You've circled one. With a little heart.
Lord Malgrin: Put that down!
Asha: How long have you been doing this job, Malgrin?
Lord Malgrin: A thousand and four years. Every decade some child with a sword climbs those stairs, and I have to do the whole speech again. Do you know how exhausting that is?
Asha: So why not retire?
Lord Malgrin: Dark lords don't retire! We get defeated. It's tradition. If I simply left, every warlord in the east would come after my throne.
Asha: Then let's make it official. I go back to the city and tell everyone I defeated you. Huge battle, lots of lightning, very dramatic.
Lord Malgrin: And in reality?
Asha: In reality, you move to Sunny Cove, the kingdom gets its rivers back, and nobody climbs your stairs ever again.
Lord Malgrin: The cottage does have a vegetable garden.
Asha: I saw. You underlined it twice.
Lord Malgrin: Very well. I accept. On one condition.
Asha: Name it.
Lord Malgrin: When the bards sing about our battle, I was at least seven feet tall. And you barely survived.

text:
Lieutenant Park: Captain, we're picking up a signal. It's coming from the fourth planet.
Captain Ortiz: The fourth planet? That's impossible. Our scans say it's completely dead. No air, no water, nothing.
Kai: Well, something down there has just said hello. It repeats every thirty seconds.
Dr. Yuen: Could it be an old probe? Some of the first missions were sent out here over a hundred years ago.
Lieutenant Park: I've checked the records. No probe has ever been sent to this system. We're the first.
Captain Ortiz: Then who's sending it? Kai, can you clean it up?
Kai: I'm trying. There's a lot of noise. It sounds like... a voice. A human voice.
Dr. Yuen: That's not possible. Unless a ship has crashed there and nobody has reported it.
Captain Ortiz: Play it.
Kai: Here we go. I've slowed it down a bit.
Lieutenant Park: It's in English. This is research ship Kestrel... do not land... repeat, do not land.
Captain Ortiz: Kestrel? Lieutenant, what's the name of this ship?
Lieutenant Park: The Kestrel, Captain. But there's only one Kestrel. Us.
Dr. Yuen: Maybe it's an echo. Our own signal, bounced back from the planet.
Kai: It can't be an echo. We haven't sent any signals for three days.
Captain Ortiz: Then play the rest. All of it.
Kai: There's a date at the end. It's... it's next Tuesday.
Dr. Yuen: Captain, I suggest we turn this ship around. Right now.
Captain Ortiz: Agreed. Park, set a course for home. Kai, what's that noise?
Kai: It's the landing system, Captain. It's just switched itself on.

o: The planet is dead, and no probe has ever been sent there
It is in an alien language

o: This is the Kestrel, do not land

title: Five Minutes, Not Six
ru: Команда в последний раз проговаривает план кражи бриллианта из музея — и один участник что-то скрывает
text:
Vera: One last time, from the beginning. Lina, the alarm.
Lina: At two fifteen I cut the cable in the basement. The whole system goes down for five minutes before the backup starts.
Vera: Tony?
Tony: I open the side door with the copy of the key. Then I wait in the van with the engine running.
Vera: Max, the diamond.
Max: I go up the stairs, take the glass off the case, swap the diamond for the fake and come back down. Six minutes.
Lina: Five. You said six again.
Max: Did I? Sorry. Five. I meant five.
Tony: That's the third time today, mate. Do you want an extra minute in prison or something?
Max: It's just a slip of the tongue. I've been awake since five this morning.
Vera: Max, have you ever been to this museum before?
Max: Once, last week. To check the stairs. Like you asked.
Vera: And did you talk to anyone while you were there?
Max: Only the woman at the ticket office. She asked if I wanted a guided tour.
Lina: Funny. The woman at the ticket office is married to a police officer. I checked.
Max: That's a coincidence. Look, what does it matter? Five, six, it's only one minute.
Vera: It matters, Max, because the police are going to be outside the museum at minute six. Aren't they?
Tony: Hold on. You've told the police?
Max: I didn't have a choice! They caught me last month. They said if I helped them, I wouldn't go to prison.
Vera: I know. That's why the real job isn't tomorrow night. It's tonight. Right now, while you're sitting here with us.
Tony: And I've already locked the door. Sorry, mate. You're staying here.

questions.q: How long is the alarm system down after Lina cuts the cable?
Who did Max talk to at the museum last week?
o: The woman at the ticket office

questions.q: What does Vera reveal at the end?
o: The real job is happening tonight, without Max

title: The Mysterious Fish
ru: Начальник собирает экстренное совещание из-за запаха рыбы в офисе — и расследование выходит из-под контроля
text:
Gary: Thank you all for coming. Please sit down. This is an emergency meeting.
Priya: Gary, it's four fifty-five on a Friday. What kind of emergency?
Gary: The worst kind. Someone in this office... has been hiding a fish.
Tom: A fish? Like a pet?
Gary: Not a pet, Tom. A dead fish. The smell started on Monday, and it's got worse every day.
Dana: He's right. I've had three complaints. One person said it smelled like a sad harbour.
Priya: So open the windows and go home. Problem solved.
Gary: No. This is about trust. I want to know who did it. Tom, where were you on Monday at lunchtime?
Tom: Me? I was eating a sandwich at my desk. Cheese and tomato. No fish at all.
Gary: That's exactly what a fish person would say.
Dana: Gary, you can't accuse people without evidence. HR has rules about this.
Gary: Fine. Then let's find some evidence. Priya, you had sushi last week.
Priya: That was two weeks ago, and I ate it. All of it. I didn't hide a piece behind the printer.
Tom: Actually, the smell is strongest in here. In this meeting room.
Dana: He's right. It's much worse near the table.
Gary: Near the table? That's ridiculous. Nobody uses this room except me.
Priya: Gary. What's in the drawer on your side of the table?
Gary: Nothing. Just some old papers and... oh no.
Tom: Is it a fish?
Gary: It's the salmon my mother gave me on Monday. I put it there so I wouldn't forget to take it home.
Priya: So you've called an emergency meeting to investigate yourself.

questions.q: When did the smell start?
Why does Gary suspect Priya?
Where was the fish?
o: In a drawer in the meeting room, on Gary's side

title: Not a Normal Night
ru: Молодой врач впервые дежурит ночью в приёмном покое, и пациент оказывается не тем, кем кажется
text:
Nurse Carla: Dr Evans? Your first patient is in bed three. Are you all right? You look pale.
Dr Evans: I'm fine. I've just never done a night shift on my own before. What's the problem?
Nurse Carla: Pain in his stomach, he says. He walked in ten minutes ago. He's very calm about it.
Dr Evans: Good evening, sir. I'm Dr Evans. Can you tell me where it hurts?
Patient: Right here, on the lower right side. It started about four hours ago near my belly button, and then it moved.
Dr Evans: That's very precise. Have you had anything to eat today?
Patient: Nothing since lunch. I haven't got a fever, but I feel a bit sick. Have you checked my temperature yet?
Dr Evans: Not yet. Carla, could you...
Nurse Carla: Already done. Thirty-seven point two. Normal.
Patient: Good. And are you going to press on my stomach, doctor? Gently, starting on the left side?
Dr Evans: Are you a doctor yourself, sir?
Patient: Me? No, no. I just watch a lot of hospital dramas.
Nurse Carla: Dr Evans, can I have a word? Over here.
Dr Evans: What is it?
Nurse Carla: He came in a taxi straight from the airport. There's a badge on his suitcase with our hospital's name on it.
Dr Evans: Our hospital? Then who is he?
Nurse Carla: I think he's Dr Hargreaves. The new head of the department. He starts on Monday.
Dr Evans: Why would the new head pretend to be ill on my first night?
Nurse Carla: To see how the night team works, I suppose. Some bosses like surprises.
Patient: I can hear you both, by the way. You've done very well, Dr Evans. Apart from one thing.
Dr Evans: What's that?
Patient: You haven't washed your hands. And this part isn't a test: the pain is real. So wash your hands and carry on, please.

Why does Nurse Carla think the patient is Dr Hargreaves?

His suitcase has a badge from their hospital

title: Gate Twelve
ru: Двое незнакомцев застряли в аэропорту из-за отменённого рейса и спорят о последнем свободном месте
text:
Announcer: Attention, please. Flight 208 to Lisbon has been cancelled. Passengers should speak to the staff at Gate Twelve.
Nora: Cancelled? No, no, no. Excuse me! I need to be in Lisbon tonight.
Clerk: I understand, madam. There's one seat left on a flight at ten tonight. After that, the next flight is at six in the morning, and it's full.
Sam: I'll take it!
Nora: Excuse me? I was here first.
Sam: You were standing here. I was standing right behind you. That's practically the same thing.
Nora: That's not how queues work. I've got a wedding tomorrow at noon. My sister's wedding.
Sam: Well, I've got a wedding tomorrow too. My best friend's. I'm the best man, and I've got the rings.
Nora: Sure you have. Everybody suddenly has a wedding when there's only one seat left.
Sam: Look, here they are. Two gold rings in a little blue box. Happy now?
Nora: Wait. A little blue box? Is your best friend called Daniel?
Sam: Yes. How do you know that?
Nora: Because my sister is marrying him. I'm the maid of honour. I've been texting Daniel about this wedding all week!
Sam: You're Nora? The Nora who sent him forty messages about the flowers?
Nora: There were problems with the flowers! Serious problems.
Clerk: Sorry to interrupt, but I need a name for this seat. Who's flying tonight?
Sam: Give it to her. The bride needs her sister more than she needs me.
Nora: But the groom needs his rings. Without them, there's no wedding.
Sam: Then take the rings with you. Problem solved.
Nora: You'd trust me with them? We met five minutes ago, and I've been shouting at you ever since.
Sam: You sent forty messages about flowers. You're clearly the most reliable person in this airport.
Clerk: Actually, another passenger has just cancelled. Now I've got two seats, right next to each other. Shall I book you together?

How are Nora and Sam connected?
o: Nora's sister is marrying Sam's best friend
They are both flying to their own weddings

A seat on the morning flight

title: The Dragon Tax
ru: Молодая королева на первом совете решает, что делать с драконом, который требует налог с королевства
text:
Queen Isolde: My lords, thank you for coming. Lord Brannock, please read the letter again.
Lord Brannock: To the new queen. Every month you will send me one hundred bags of gold. If you don't, I will burn your wheat fields. Kind regards, Vorgath.
General Maro: Kind regards? The beast is laughing at us, Your Majesty. Give me two hundred soldiers, and I'll bring you its head.
Lord Brannock: Your last two hundred soldiers came back without their eyebrows, General.
General Maro: That was a different dragon. A smaller one.
Queen Isolde: And how much gold have we actually got, Lord Brannock?
Lord Brannock: Enough for three months. After that, we'll have to sell the castle furniture. Starting with your throne.
Queen Isolde: So we can't fight, and we can't pay. Wonderful. Has anyone got an idea that doesn't end in disaster?
Mira: I might, Your Majesty. If I'm allowed to speak.
General Maro: The librarian? This is a war council, girl, not a reading club.
Queen Isolde: Let her speak, General. Go on, Mira.
Mira: I've read every book in the library about dragons. They don't spend gold. They sleep on it, because metal holds heat and their caves are freezing.
Lord Brannock: So the dragon doesn't want to be rich. It wants to be warm?
Mira: Exactly. And the old mines under the Red Hills are full of hot springs. The rocks there never go cold.
Queen Isolde: So instead of gold, we offer Vorgath a new home. A warm one.
General Maro: And if the dragon says no?
Mira: Then we've lost nothing but a letter. Besides, there's something on the back that Lord Brannock didn't read.
Lord Brannock: Is there? Oh. Very small writing at the bottom.
Queen Isolde: Read it, please.
Lord Brannock: P.S. It's really very cold up here.

According to Mira, why do dragons sleep on gold?
o: Metal holds heat, and their caves are cold

title: The Wrong Name on the Cup
ru: Друзья в кафе пытаются помочь приятелю, который месяц не может признаться бариста, что его зовут не Кевин
text:
Jess: Okay, he's coming back from the counter. Look at his face.
Leo: Let me guess. It says Kevin again.
Omar: It says Kevin again. With a little smiley face this time.
Jess: Omar, it's been a month. You've drunk about forty coffees as Kevin.
Omar: I know! The first time, I thought it was a mistake. By the third time, it was too late to say anything.
Leo: Why too late? You just say: Sorry, my name's actually Omar.
Omar: Because yesterday she said: Kevin, you're my favourite customer! How do I come back from that?
Jess: So you're going to be Kevin forever? What if you two get married?
Omar: We are not getting married. We've talked about the weather twice.
Leo: Twice! That's basically engaged.
Jess: Right. Here's the plan. You go up there and order a muffin, and when she says Kevin, you correct her. Calmly.
Omar: And what if she's embarrassed?
Leo: Then she'll be embarrassed for five seconds, instead of you being Kevin for fifty years.
Omar: Fine. Fine! I'm going.
Barista: Hi again, Kevin! Something else?
Omar: Hi. A blueberry muffin, please. And, um... actually, my name isn't Kevin. It's Omar.
Barista: Oh, I know.
Omar: You know?
Barista: You paid by card on your first day. It says Omar on it. I just wanted to see how long it would take you to say something.
Omar: A month. It took me a month.
Barista: Thirty-one days, actually. We had a bet behind the counter. Oh, and my name isn't Sarah, by the way. I just found this badge in a drawer.

What is Jess's plan?

Omar should find a new cafe

title: The Witness Who Saw Too Much
ru: Адвокат защиты разбирает показания уверенного свидетеля и находит деталь, которая переворачивает дело
text:
Judge Whitmore: Ms. Adeyemi, your witness.
Ms. Adeyemi: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Crane, you told the prosecution you saw my client leave the warehouse at eleven fifteen on the night of the fourteenth.
Crane: That's right. I'd stake my life on it.
Ms. Adeyemi: Let's hope it doesn't come to that. Where exactly were you standing?
Crane: Across the street, outside the launderette. Waiting for my washing.
Ms. Adeyemi: At eleven o'clock at night?
Crane: It's cheaper after ten. I'm not made of money.
Ms. Adeyemi: Fair enough. And it was dark, I assume?
Crane: There's a streetlamp right by the warehouse door. She walked straight under it.
Ms. Adeyemi: You'd never met my client before. So how did you recognise her?
Crane: The hair. Bright red, down to her shoulders. You don't forget hair like that.
Ms. Adeyemi: Bright red. You're certain of the colour?
Crane: As certain as I am of my own name.
Ms. Adeyemi: Your Honour, I'd like to submit Exhibit D. A receipt from a hair salon on Mill Road.
Judge Whitmore: Go on.
Ms. Adeyemi: It's dated the twentieth, six days after the robbery. It's for a full colour change, from blonde to red.
Crane: So what? Maybe she dyed it twice.
Ms. Adeyemi: Then let's look at Exhibit E. A still from the security camera at her office, taken on the morning of the fifteenth.
Prosecutor: Objection, Your Honour. Counsel is ambushing the witness.
Judge Whitmore: Overruled. I'd quite like to see it myself.
Ms. Adeyemi: Pale blonde, as you can see. So, Mr. Crane, when did you first see my client with red hair?
Crane: I... In the paper. There was a photo of her after the arrest.
Ms. Adeyemi: So the woman you remember is the woman from the newspaper.
Crane: I saw someone that night. I know I did.
Ms. Adeyemi: I don't doubt it, Mr. Crane. I just doubt it was her. No further questions.

o: He was waiting for a friend

o: The defendant was at her office on the night of the robbery
The defendant only dyed her hair red after the robbery

title: Off the Record
ru: Советник пытается убедить министра замять утечку документов, но у министра свои планы
text:
Hollis: Minister, have you seen the papers?
Minister Kerr: I've seen my phone, which is worse. Forty missed calls before seven. Who leaked it?
Hollis: We don't know yet. But whoever it was knew exactly what they were doing. Front page, the full contract, your signature at the bottom.
Minister Kerr: My signature is on a great many things, Hollis. That's rather the job.
Hollis: Not usually on a two-billion-pound defence deal with a company owned by the Prime Minister's brother-in-law.
Minister Kerr: When you put it like that, it does sound unfortunate.
Hollis: Here's what I suggest. We say the document is an early draft. Unsigned, unofficial, taken out of context.
Minister Kerr: It has my signature on it.
Hollis: Signatures can be copied. We hint at a forgery, we keep it vague, and by Friday the papers have moved on to something else.
Minister Kerr: You've given this a lot of thought for someone who found out an hour ago.
Hollis: It's my job to think fast. The Prime Minister's office wants a statement by ten.
Minister Kerr: I'm sure it does. Tell me, Hollis, who do you think benefits from this story?
Hollis: The opposition, obviously. The press. Anyone who wants your job.
Minister Kerr: Or anyone who didn't want that contract to go ahead in the first place.
Hollis: I'm not sure I follow.
Minister Kerr: I was told to sign that deal, Hollis. Told, not asked. Three days later, I was told to forget I'd ever seen it.
Hollis: Minister... please tell me you didn't.
Minister Kerr: Officially, I have no idea how that document reached the Courier.
Hollis: And unofficially?
Minister Kerr: Unofficially, the deal is dead, the brother-in-law is ringing his lawyers, and the Prime Minister has bigger problems than me.
Hollis: You realise that if anyone finds out, you're finished.
Minister Kerr: Which is why I'll need that statement after all. Something about a forgery, I think. You were very convincing.

It was signed by Hollis without permission
It shows the Minister took a bribe

o: Claiming the document is an early draft or a forgery

o: The Prime Minister wants to cancel the deal

title: Nobody Lives Upstairs
ru: Пара переезжает в дешёвый старый дом, и первая ночь начинается со странных звуков сверху
text:
Dan: Well, it's no palace, but for this price I'm not complaining.
Rachel: That's exactly what worries me. Houses this big don't go for peanuts unless there's a catch.
Dan: The catch is the plumbing. The agent told us. And the wallpaper, which is frankly a crime.
Rachel: The agent also wouldn't come past the front door. Did you notice? She threw the keys at me like they were on fire.
Dan: She had another viewing. Estate agents are always in a rush.
Rachel: At eight o'clock at night? Wait. What was that?
Dan: What was what?
Rachel: Upstairs. It sounded like someone dragging a chair across the floor.
Dan: Old houses creak, love. The wood settles when it gets cold.
Rachel: Wood doesn't settle in a straight line from one end of the room to the other.
Dan: Fine. I'll go and have a look. Pass me the torch.
Rachel: You're not going up there on your own.
Dan: You're right. You're coming with me.
Rachel: That's not what I meant, and you know it.
Dan: Okay. Top of the stairs. There's a little door here. Must be the attic. It's locked.
Rachel: Then leave it locked. Some doors are locked for a reason.
Dan: The key's in it. On our side. Who locks a door and leaves the key on the outside?
Rachel: Someone who wanted to keep something in, Dan. Not out.
Dan: Right, I'm opening it. It's just boxes. Boxes, a rocking chair, and... a cup of tea.
Rachel: A cup of tea?
Dan: It's warm. Rachel, it's still warm.
Rachel: We're leaving. Now. I don't care about the deposit.
Voice: Would you mind closing the door on your way out? There's a terrible draught.

title: The Wrong Umbrella
ru: Встреча двух агентов на вокзале идёт не по плану: пароль не совпадает, а время на исходе
text:
Agent Novak: Is this seat taken?
Elise: That depends. Do you prefer tea or coffee when it rains?
Agent Novak: Neither. I prefer the rain in Lisbon.
Elise: Wrong answer. The correct reply is “only in Vienna”. Sit down anyway, before you draw attention to us.
Agent Novak: They changed the phrase last night. Didn't you get the message?
Elise: I don't get messages. That's rather the point of what I do. Who sent you?
Agent Novak: The usual people. Grey building, terrible coffee. And you're carrying a blue umbrella.
Elise: Very observant. It's raining. Lots of people carry umbrellas.
Agent Novak: I was told green. Green umbrella, table by the window, quarter past four.
Elise: And I was told a man with a newspaper folded in three. Yours is folded in half.
Agent Novak: It's a big newspaper. It didn't want to be folded in three.
Elise: Charming. The train to Prague leaves in six minutes. The package has to be on it, and I don't hand it to strangers.
Agent Novak: I'm not a stranger. We met in Brussels two years ago. You threw a croissant at a man in a hat.
Elise: Half the agents in Europe have heard that story.
Agent Novak: Fine. Ask me something only the real contact would know.
Elise: What's in the package?
Agent Novak: If I knew that, they wouldn't need either of us.
Elise: Good answer. Annoyingly good. Four minutes.
Agent Novak: Don't look now, but the table behind you. A woman with a green umbrella. And a man with a newspaper folded in three.
Elise: Oh, no.
Agent Novak: They're staring at us. And they look just as confused as we are.
Elise: So we've both been trying to convince the wrong spy.
Agent Novak: Shall we swap tables, or just swap partners?
Elise: Swap tables. Quickly. And Novak? Learn to fold a newspaper.

title: The Announcement
ru: Воскресный ужин, на котором каждый член семьи пытается сообщить свою новость — и никто не хочет быть первым
text:
Margaret: Isn't this lovely? All of us round one table. It only took a year and a half.
Tom: Mum, you say that every time. It's been four months.
Margaret: Four months is a long time at my age. Pass the potatoes, Claire.
Claire: Here. So, Dad, you said on the phone you had something to tell us.
Richard: Did I? I don't think I said that. Your mother said that.
Margaret: I said no such thing. I said your father had been acting strangely. That's different.
Tom: How strangely?
Margaret: He goes out every Tuesday and comes home smelling of petrol.
Richard: Can we talk about something else? Tom, how's work?
Tom: Work's... fine. Actually, funny you should ask. I've got some news too.
Claire: Oh, thank God. You go first.
Tom: Why? What's yours?
Claire: Nothing. Go on.
Tom: No, no. You clearly have something. Ladies first.
Claire: That's not how that works, and you know it.
Margaret: Will somebody please say something before the gravy goes cold?
Claire: Fine! Ben proposed. We're getting married in June.
Margaret: Oh, darling! That's wonderful news!
Tom: Great, now nobody's going to care about mine. I've quit the law firm. I'm opening a food truck.
Richard: A food truck? Thank goodness. I thought I'd be the only one.
Claire: The only one what?
Richard: That's where I go on Tuesdays. Motorbike lessons. I passed my test on Friday.
Margaret: A motorbike. At sixty-eight. I married a teenager.
Tom: Mum, what about you? Haven't you got any news?
Margaret: Only that Ben rang your father to ask for permission three weeks ago. I've known ever since. That “Oh, darling!” took me ages to rehearse.

title: Two Sources or Nothing
ru: Молодая журналистка приносит редактору сенсацию за час до сдачи номера, но источник всего один
text:
Fiona: Walt, have you got a minute?
Walt: I've got fifty-three minutes till we go to print, and every single one of them is spoken for. What is it?
Fiona: The water company. I've cracked it. They knew about the contamination for two years and buried the report.
Walt: That's a big claim. How do you know?
Fiona: I've got an insider. A senior engineer. She gave me the internal emails, the lab results, everything.
Walt: One insider.
Fiona: One very good insider.
Walt: Fiona, you know the rule. Two independent sources, or it doesn't run. I don't care if your source is the Archbishop of Canterbury.
Fiona: The emails are the second source! They're right here, in black and white.
Walt: Emails she gave you. If she's got an axe to grind and she faked them, we're finished. Not just you. The whole paper.
Fiona: She hasn't got an axe to grind. She's terrified. Her kids drink that water.
Walt: Which makes her sympathetic. It doesn't make her right.
Fiona: If we wait a week, someone else gets the story. Or the company finds out she talked to us.
Walt: Then find me someone else in the next forty minutes. Anyone who can confirm that report exists.
Fiona: In forty minutes? Who am I supposed to call at nine o'clock at night?
Walt: Hold that thought. I need to take this call.
Fiona: Now? Seriously? ...Well? Who was it?
Walt: That was the water company's head of communications. Apparently they've heard rumours that we're running a story.
Fiona: How on earth have they heard that?
Walt: No idea. But she asked me, very politely, not to mention the 2022 lab report.
Fiona: But I never told anyone outside this room about a lab report.
Walt: And they've just asked us not to print it. Which means it's real. Congratulations, Fiona. They've just become your second source.
Fiona: So it runs?
Walt: Front page. You've got thirty-five minutes. Stop standing there and write.

title: Performance Review
ru: Супергероиня проходит ежегодную аттестацию у бюрократа из отдела кадров — и спасение мира в показатели не входит
text:
Mr. Pembleton: Please, take a seat. Gently, if possible. We've had issues with chairs.
Nova: That was one chair. And it was during an earthquake.
Mr. Pembleton: Which you caused.
Nova: Which I stopped. There's a difference.
Mr. Pembleton: Let's not get bogged down in details. This is your annual performance review, and I'll be frank. The numbers aren't great.
Nova: I saved the city four times this year. Five, if you count the thing with the giant bees.
Mr. Pembleton: Saving the city isn't one of our key performance indicators.
Nova: What? What else is there?
Mr. Pembleton: Paperwork, mostly. You've filed three incident reports out of a possible forty-one.
Nova: I was busy with the incidents.
Mr. Pembleton: Then there's property damage. Two bridges, one shopping centre and a statue of the mayor.
Nova: The statue was an accident. The head came off when I landed on it.
Mr. Pembleton: Customer satisfaction is also down. We received a complaint from a gentleman you rescued from a burning building.
Nova: A complaint? I carried him out of the fire!
Mr. Pembleton: By the ankle. Upside down. He says he lost his reading glasses and his dignity.
Nova: Look, Mr. Pembleton, with respect, I didn't become a superhero to fill in forms.
Mr. Pembleton: None of us end up where we expected, Nova. I wanted to be an astronaut.
Nova: What happened?
Mr. Pembleton: Forms. Now, about your targets for next year. I'd like to see fewer explosions and more—
Nova: Hold on. That's the alarm. Something's attacking the harbour.
Mr. Pembleton: We haven't finished. Leaving a review early requires a signed Form 12C.
Nova: I'll fill it in on the way down.
Mr. Pembleton: On the way down? Nova, the door's over— And that's another window. Wonderful.

title: The Stranger at the Bar
ru: В салун маленького городка входит незнакомец, и хозяйка быстро понимает, что он приехал не за виски
text:
Ada: Evening, stranger. You look like you've been riding since last Tuesday.
Stranger: Since Sunday. Coffee, if you've got it. Black.
Ada: This is a saloon, mister. Coffee's what we serve to folks who've given up on life.
Stranger: Then it'll suit me fine.
Ada: Coming right up. Passing through, or planning to stay?
Stranger: Depends on what I find. I'm looking for a man called Harlan Reed.
Ada: Never heard of him.
Stranger: That's funny. You answered before I'd finished saying his name.
Ada: I've got a quick tongue. Ask anyone in town.
Stranger: The fella at the stables says Reed comes in here every Friday. Sits in the corner, plays cards, loses.
Ada: The fella at the stables talks a lot for a man who can't count his own horses.
Stranger: Ma'am, I'll be honest with you. I've ridden four hundred miles to find Harlan Reed. I'm not leaving without him.
Ada: Men who ride four hundred miles for somebody usually bring a rope. Or a gun.
Stranger: I've got a gun. Everybody's got a gun. That's not why I'm here.
Ada: Then why are you here?
Stranger: Paperwork. His aunt passed away in Kansas City last spring. She left him her house, her land and five thousand dollars.
Ada: Five thousand?
Stranger: In gold. All he has to do is sign. But if I can't find him by the end of the month, it all goes to the church.
Ada: Well. Now that you mention it, the name does ring a bell.
Stranger: Does it, now.
Ada: Harlan Reed. Tall, terrible at cards, snores like a train. He's my husband.
Stranger: Your husband. You told me you'd never heard of him.
Ada: A woman can't be too careful, mister. The last three men who came asking were bounty hunters. Harlan! Get down here! And put on your good shirt!

title: A Boy Alone at Christmas
ru: Мальчик один дома на Рождество — и два неудачливых вора
text:
A big family. A big house near Chicago. A trip to Paris for Christmas. And one small problem: they forget one child at home.

Home Alone came out in 1990. Chris Columbus directed it, and John Hughes wrote it. Macaulay Culkin plays Kevin McCallister, an eight-year-old boy. The night before the trip, Kevin is angry with his family, and he makes a wish: he wants them all to disappear. The next morning, the family is late. Everybody runs to the airport... and nobody counts the kids.

At first, Kevin is happy. He eats junk food and jumps on his parents' bed. He tries his father's aftershave. It burns his face, and he screams with both hands on his cheeks. This picture of Kevin is famous all over the world.

But then two thieves come to the street: Harry and Marv. They want to rob the empty houses, and Kevin's house is next. Kevin is small, but he is smart. He gets the house ready: toys on the floor, paint cans on ropes and a very, very hot door handle.

In Paris, his mother does everything to get home to her son.

The film was a huge success, and in many countries it is now a Christmas tradition. Families watch it every winter — and then count their children twice.

title: Dinosaurs Are Back
ru: Парк с настоящими динозаврами на острове — что может пойти не так?
text:
A rich old man has a dream. On an island near Costa Rica, he builds a park with real, living dinosaurs. What can go wrong? Everything.

Jurassic Park came out in 1993. Steven Spielberg directed it, and the story comes from a book by Michael Crichton. The rich man is John Hammond. Before the park opens, he invites a few scientists and his two grandchildren to see it.

How do you make a dinosaur? In the film, scientists find very old mosquitoes in amber — old, hard tree juice, yellow like honey. Millions of years ago, these mosquitoes drank dinosaur blood. From this blood, the scientists take dinosaur DNA.

The dinosaurs look amazingly real. Some are big robots, and some are computer pictures. In 1993 people in cinemas could not believe their eyes. Do you remember the glass of water on the table? The water moves — boom, boom — because something huge is coming. That is the T. rex.

But the scariest animals are the velociraptors. They are fast and smart, and they hunt in groups. Here is a fun fact: real velociraptors were much smaller, about the size of a turkey.

The film was the biggest hit of its time, and many children loved dinosaurs because of it. Maybe you were one of them.

o: In a big city in America
On an island near Costa Rica

title: Love on a Big Ship
ru: История любви на знаменитом корабле «Титаник»
text:
Everybody knows how this story ends. The ship sinks. And still millions of people went to see the film, many of them again and again.

Titanic came out in 1997. James Cameron wrote and directed it. The real Titanic, a huge British ship, hit an iceberg — a mountain of ice in the sea — in April 1912. It went down in the cold Atlantic Ocean. More than a thousand people died.

The film tells a love story on this ship. Rose (Kate Winslet) is a young woman in first class. Her family needs money, so they want her to marry a rich man, and she is unhappy. Jack (Leonardo DiCaprio) is a poor artist. He won his ticket in a card game, a few minutes before the ship left. They fall in love. But they have only a few days.

The film has famous moments. Jack stands at the front of the ship, opens his arms and shouts, “I'm the king of the world!” Later Rose stands there with her arms open, and she feels like she is flying. And Celine Dion sings “My Heart Will Go On” — a song that was everywhere.

Titanic won eleven Oscars, and for many years it was the biggest film in history. Cameron loves the sea: he went down to the real Titanic many times.

title: A Bear in London
ru: Вежливый медвежонок из Перу приезжает в Лондон
text:
A small bear is sitting at a London railway station. He has a red hat and an old suitcase. Around his neck there is a label: “Please look after this bear. Thank you.”

The bear comes from Peru, from the deep jungle. His aunt Lucy and uncle Pastuzo always loved London. They told him that people there are kind to strangers. Now he is here. But London is cold, busy and not very friendly.

Then the Brown family finds him. Mr Brown is nervous and careful. Mrs Brown has a big heart. They take the bear home, just for one night, and give him a name: Paddington, like the station.

Paddington is very polite, but he brings trouble everywhere. On his first evening in the house, he floods the bathroom. And there is a dangerous woman, Millicent. She works at a museum, and she wants Paddington there, in a glass box — and not alive.

The film came out in 2014. Paul King directed it, and Ben Whishaw is the voice of Paddington. The bear himself is much older: Michael Bond wrote the first book about him in 1958.

One last secret: Paddington loves marmalade, a jam made from oranges. He always keeps a marmalade sandwich under his hat. For emergencies.

Where does his name come from?
o: From a book in the house

title: A Car That Travels in Time
ru: Подросток на машине времени попадает в молодость своих родителей
text:
What would you do if you could meet your parents when they were teenagers? In Back to the Future, seventeen-year-old Marty McFly finds out, and it's much harder than it sounds.

The film came out in 1985. Robert Zemeckis directed it, Steven Spielberg was one of the producers, and Michael J. Fox played Marty. Christopher Lloyd played his friend Doc Brown, a crazy scientist with wild white hair.

Doc builds a time machine, and he builds it out of a car: a silver DeLorean with doors that open upwards like wings. Why a car? Because it looks cool, of course. When the car reaches 88 miles per hour, it jumps through time.

One night something goes wrong, and Marty has to escape in the DeLorean. Suddenly he is in 1955, in his own small town, thirty years in the past. He doesn't have the special fuel for the trip home, so he is stuck. Then he meets his future mom and dad, who are high school students. His dad is shy and weak. His mom is... very interested in Marty. That is a big problem: if his parents don't fall in love, Marty will never be born. In a photo of Marty with his brother and sister, the faces slowly begin to disappear.

Here is a surprising fact: Michael J. Fox was not the first Marty. Another actor, Eric Stoltz, played the role for several weeks before the filmmakers decided to start again with Fox.

Back to the Future was the biggest hit of 1985 in America. Two sequels followed, and the DeLorean became one of the most famous cars in movie history.
